(p. 722; p. 723)

The meaning is that He does not take away a blessing He has bestowed on a people until they change what is within themselves of goodness and righteous deeds, or change the natural disposition (*fitrah*, the innate human nature) in which Allah created them.

It has been said: the intended meaning is not that He never sends a punishment upon any of His servants unless a sin has preceded it from that person. Rather, calamities may befall people because of the sins of others, as in the hadith that a questioner asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "Will we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us?" He said, "Yes, when corruption becomes widespread." ﴿And when Allah wills harm for a people﴾, that is, destruction and punishment, ﴿there is no turning it back﴾, that is, there is no one to repel it. It has also been said that the meaning is: when Allah wills harm for a people, He blinds their hearts until they choose that which brings affliction upon them. ﴿And they have no protector besides Him﴾ who would take charge of their affairs and whom they could seek refuge with, so that he might ward off from them the punishment that comes to them from Allah, the Glorified, or no helper who would aid them and prevent them from the punishment of Allah.

The meaning is: there is no one who can repel the punishment of Allah, nor anyone who can annul His judgment.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿And if you marvel, then marvelous is their saying﴾: he said, "If you marvel, O Muhammad, at their denial of you, then marvelous is their saying."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning the verse, he said: "If you marvel, O Muhammad, at their denial, though they have seen the power and command of Allah, and the parables He has set forth for them, and what He has shown them of the giving of life to the dead and to the dead earth ﴿then marvelous is their saying: 'When we have become dust, will we truly be in a new creation?'﴾ Do they not see that He created them from a drop of semen? Creating from a drop of semen is greater than creating from dust and bones."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿And exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾: he said, "The punishments."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah concerning the *mathulat* (exemplary punishments): he said, "They are the events of Allah among the nations concerning those who passed before you."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The *mathulat* are the punishments that befell the earlier generations."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing, and indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Were it not for the pardon of Allah and His overlooking, no one would enjoy a pleasant life; and were it not for His warning and His punishment, everyone would become complacent.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and for every people there is a guide﴾: he said, "A caller."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people a guide﴾: he said, "The warner is Muhammad (ﷺ), and ﴿for every people a guide﴾ is a prophet who calls them to Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "Muhammad is the warner, and the guide is Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid something similar as well.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the warner and he is the guide."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah and Abu al-Duha something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah*, al-Daylami, Ibn Asakir and Ibn al-Najjar narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people a guide﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed his hand upon his chest and said, 'I am the warner,' and he gestured with his hand toward the shoulder of Ali and said, 'You are the guide, O Ali; through you will be guided those who are guided after me.'" Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "This hadith contains severe objectionable content."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Barzah al-Aslami, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in *al-Mukhtarah* narrated from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well.

Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Musnad*, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning the verse something similar as well.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾: he said, "Every female among the creatures of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning the verse: he said, "He knows whether it is male or female." ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "It is the woman who sees blood during her pregnancy."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "The flow of blood." ﴿And what they increase﴾: he said, "Its retention."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "That she sees blood during her pregnancy." ﴿And what they increase﴾: he said, "In nine months." Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated through the route of al-Dahhak from him concerning the verse, he said: "What they increase beyond nine, and what they lose of the nine."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him concerning the verse ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "The miscarriage." ﴿And what they increase﴾: "What they add to the pregnancy beyond what they lost, until they give birth to it complete."

This is because among women there is one who carries for ten months, and among them one who carries for nine months, and among them one whose pregnancy is shorter.

So that is the diminishing and the increasing that Allah mentioned, and Allah, the Exalted, knows all of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning His words ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾: he said, "The secret and the public."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated concerning His words ﴿And whoever hides his speech at night or goes forth by day﴾: he said, "One who rides his head into sins." ﴿And one who goes forth freely by day﴾: he said, "One who openly commits sins by day."

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, ﴿and one who goes forth freely by day﴾: he said, "The open one." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "He is a person of suspicion who hides at night, and when he goes out by day he makes people think he is free of sin."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Kabir*, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il* narrated through the route of Ata' ibn Yasar from Ibn Abbas that the occasion of revelation of the verse was the arrival of Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Qays before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the well-known account, and that when Amir ibn al-Tufayl was afflicted with the plague (*ghuddah*), the words of Allah, the Exalted, were revealed: ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾ up to His words ﴿with angels following one another before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah﴾. He said: "The ones following one another by the command of Allah guard Muhammad (ﷺ)." Then he mentioned Arbad ibn Qays and what killed him, and He said: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾ up to His words ﴿and He is mighty in strength﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿with angels following one another﴾, the verse, he said: "This is specifically for the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿guarding him by the command of Allah﴾, he said: "That guarding is by the command of Allah, by the command of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him ﴿by the command of Allah﴾, he said: "By the permission of Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning the verse, he said: "The ruler's close attendants, who have guards around him, guarding him from before him and behind him." He means: they guard him from My command; for when I will harm a people, there is no turning it back.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "Kings take guards who protect him from in front of him, behind him, to his right and to his left, guarding him from being killed. Have you not heard that Allah says: ﴿But when Allah wills harm for a people, there is no turning it back﴾? That is, if He wills harm, the guards will not avail him anything."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah concerning the verse, he said: "These are the commanders."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They are the angels who follow one another by night, writing down about the son of Adam."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "Angels who guard him from before him and behind him; when the decree of Allah comes, they leave him alone."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ali concerning the verse, he said: "There is no servant except that with him are angels who guard him from a wall falling upon him, or from falling into a well, or from being eaten by a predator, or from drowning or burning. When the decree comes, they leave between him and the decree." Numerous hadiths have been transmitted concerning the mention of the guardians (*hafazah*) assigned to a human being, mentioned in the books of hadith.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 13, verses 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying﴾. That is, if you are amazed, O Muhammad, at their denial of you after you were among them as one known for truthfulness, then more amazing is their denial of the Resurrection.

Allah, exalted is He, cannot be described as being amazed (ta'ajjub), because amazement is a change in the soul caused by something whose causes are hidden. He mentioned it so that His Messenger and his followers would be amazed by it.

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, this matter is also astonishing, that they deny the Resurrection, while He has shown them, through the creation of the heavens and the earth, what proves that resurrection is easier in terms of power. It was also said: the verse concerns those who deny the Creator. That is, if you are amazed at their denial of the Creator despite the clear proofs that what changes must have a changer, then that is the object of amazement. But the first interpretation is preferable because of His saying: ﴿When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ This sentence is in the place of nominative case (raf') as a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitution) for their saying. It is permissible for it to be in the place of accusative case (nasb) as the object of the verb "said" (maqul al-qawl). According to the first view, the amazement refers to their own speech; according to the second, it refers to their speaking that way. The governing element of idha ("when") is what is implied by His saying ﴿Will we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, which is "we will be raised" or "we will be returned."

Their question is one of denial, which expresses the utmost remoteness of the idea. The fronting of the adverbial phrase in His saying ﴿in a new creation﴾ emphasizes the denial of resurrection. Likewise, the repetition of the hamza (interrogative particle) in His saying: a'idha (ʾa-ʾinnā), i.e., ﴿Are we…? Are we…?﴾

Then, when Allah, glorified is He, related that about them, He passed judgment on them concerning three matters. The first: ﴿They are those who disbelieved in their Lord﴾. That is, those who deny His power to resurrect are those who persist in disbelief and are complete in it.

The second: ﴿And they will have shackles around their necks﴾. Al-aghlal (shackles) is the plural of ghull, which is a collar by which the hand is tied to the neck. That is, they will be shackled with them on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the shackles are their evil deeds, which cling to them as collars cling to necks.

The third: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾, never leaving it under any circumstances. The placement of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) indicates that eternal abiding is specific to those who deny the Resurrection.

﴿And they ask you to hasten evil before good﴾. The evil (al-sayyi'ah) is the destroying punishment. The good (al-hasanah) is well-being and safety. They said this statement out of their extreme denial, their intense resolve, and their obsession with disbelief. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is that they requested punishment before good, which is faith.

﴿And there have already occurred before them the exemplary punishments (al-mathulat)﴾. The majority of readers recited mathulat with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the thaʾ, the plural of mathulah, like samurah, which means punishment. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-mathulah is a punishment that leaves a blemish on the one punished by altering some part of his form, from the saying: "Fulan mutilated Fulan" when he disfigured his body by cutting off his nose, gouging out his eyes, or ripping open his belly.

Al-A'mash recited it with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the thaʾ, for lightness, since the damma is heavy. In the dialect of Tamim it is with a damma on both the mim and the thaʾ. Its singular in their dialect is muthlah, with a damma on the mim and a sukun on the thaʾ, like ghurfah and ghurufat.

It is also reported from al-A'mash in another narration that he recited this word with a damma on it, according to the dialect of Tamim.

The meaning: these people ask you to hasten the sending of punishment upon them, although punishments of their like among the deniers have already passed before them. So why do they not take warning from them and beware of what befell those others? The sentence is in the place of accusative case as a circumstantial clause (hal). This hastening by these people is in the manner of mockery, like their saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You…﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], to the end of the verse.

﴿And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness﴾, that is, full of great pardon, ﴿toward people despite their wrongdoing﴾ against themselves by committing sins and falling into disobedience, if they repent from that and return to Allah, glorified is He. The prepositional phrase, i.e., "despite their wrongdoing," is in the place of accusative case as a circumstantial clause, meaning while they are wrongdoers. The particle ʿalā here has the meaning of maʿa ("with"), i.e., "with their wrongdoing." In the verse there is a great glad tiding and a great hope, because it is known that a person while engaged in wrongdoing is not repentant. For this reason it was said that it refers specifically to the sinners among the monotheists. It was also said: the forgiveness mentioned here means the delay of punishment until the Hereafter, to match what Allah related of the disbelievers' hastening for punishment, as the sentence mentioned after this verse indicates, namely: ﴿And indeed, your Lord is severe in punishment﴾, He punishes the disobedient deniers among the disbelievers with severe punishment in the Hereafter, according to what His will requires.

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ That is, why has a sign other than what he has already brought of the signs not been sent down upon him? These disbelievers who make this statement are the ones who hasten for the punishment.

Al-Zajjaj said: They requested signs other than those he had brought, so they sought the like of the signs of Moses and Jesus. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿You are only a warner﴾, warning them of the Fire, and no sign is in your hands. End of quote.

This is arrogance and obstinacy on the part of the disbelievers, since Allah had indeed sent down to His Messenger signs sufficient for those who are guided. The phrase ﴿You are only a warner﴾ comes in the form of restriction (hasr) to show that he, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, is a messenger for warning the servants and for explaining what they should beware of as its consequence, and that there is nothing else incumbent upon him beyond that.

He has done what is incumbent upon him: he warned with the most eloquent warning, and he left nothing by which that warning is achieved without bringing it, clarifying it, and repeating it.

May Allah reward him on behalf of his community with goodness.

﴿And for every people is a guide﴾, that is, a prophet who calls them to what contains their guidance and right direction, even if guidance does not actually reach them and they do not accept it. The signs of the messengers differ: one brings a sign or signs that another did not bring, according to what Allah gives of them. Whoever demands from some of them what another brought has reached an enormous level of obstinacy. Therefore, the purpose of signs is only to indicate prophethood, since they are miracles beyond human capacity, and that does not restrict to any single one of them, nor to specific individuals.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿And for every people is a guide﴾ is that the guide is Allah, mighty and majestic is He, for He is capable of that, and upon His prophets is only the mere warning.

﴿Allah knows what every female carries﴾. This sentence is resumptive (mustanʾafah), brought to show His comprehensive knowledge, glorified is He, and His knowledge of the unseen of which these matters mentioned are part.

It was said: it is also permissible that the noble name (Allah) is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "And for every people is a guide, and he is Allah." The sentence ﴿knows what every female carries﴾ would then be an explanation of "guide" according to the last view. But this is very far-fetched. Here, "mā" (what) is a relative pronoun, meaning: He knows that which every female carries in her womb, whether a clot, or a lump of flesh, or male or female, or beautiful or ugly, or fortunate or wretched.

It is also permissible that it be an interrogative (istifhamiyyah), meaning: He knows what thing is in her womb and in what state it is.

It is also permissible that it be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), meaning: He knows her carrying.

﴿And what the wombs decrease and what they increase﴾. Al-ghayd means decrease. That is, He knows what the wombs decrease, i.e., diminish, and He knows what they increase.

It was said: the intended meaning is the decrease in the formation of the fetus and its increase, such as the decrease of a finger or its increase. It was said: the intended meaning is the decrease in the duration of pregnancy below nine months, or its increase. It was said: if a woman menstruates while pregnant, that is a decrease in her child. It was said: al-ghayd is what the wombs diminish of blood, and the increase is what they add to it. The particle mā in "what they decrease and what they increase" admits the three possibilities mentioned earlier concerning "what every female carries."

﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾, that is, everything among the things of which those mentioned are part is with Allah, glorified is He, in measure. Measure (miqdar) is the extent that Allah has ordained. This is the meaning of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, all things We have created in measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49], that is, all things with Allah, glorified is He, proceed according to His decree which has already preceded and been finished, and nothing departs from that.

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, that is, Knower of everything absent from the senses and everything present and witnessed, or Knower of everything nonexistent and existent. There is no obstacle to interpreting the statement as including what is more general than that.

﴿The Great, the Most High﴾, that is, the Magnificent, before whom everything is lesser, the Exalted above what the polytheists say, or the One who is高 above everything by His power, majesty, and dominion.

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned that He knows those unseen matters, none of which escapes Him, He explained that He knows what they conceal within themselves and what they proclaim to others, and that this is not different to Him. So He said: ﴿Whether one of you conceals speech or openly speaks it﴾. So He knows what a person conceals just as He knows what he openly does, whether good or evil.

His saying "among you" (minkum) is connected to "equal" (sawa'), meaning: "the one who conceals and the one who openly declares are equal among you," or "the secret of the one who conceals and the open speech of the one who speaks openly."

﴿And whoever is hidden by night﴾, that is, concealed in the darkness that exists at night, hiding from eyes. It is said: "the thing was hidden" (khafiya) and "he hid himself" (istakhfa), meaning he concealed himself and hid. ﴿And one who goes freely by day﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: sariba yasrubu sarban and suruban means he went away, and from this is the poet's saying:

Every people has gathered around the tether of its stallion, but we have loosed its tether, so it is free to go.

That is, it went away.

Al-Qutaybi said: sarib by day means one who moves about freely in his needs with speed, from the saying "the water flowed away" (asraba al-ma').

Al-Asma'i said: sarabuhu means his path or way.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: the one who is openly manifest in speech, the one who conceals in his soul, the one who appears in the roads, and the one who hides in the darkness are all equally known to Allah. This is closest to the meaning of the verse, as the contrast between "the one who hides" and "the one who goes freely" indicates: the one who hides is the one concealed, and the one who goes freely is the one who is manifest and visible.

﴿For him there are successive (mu'aqqibat) [angels]﴾. The pronoun in "for him" refers to "whoever" in His saying: ﴿whether one of you conceals speech or openly speaks it, and whoever is hidden﴾. That is, for each of these there are mu'aqqibat. The mu'aqqibat are those who alternate, each of whom succeeds the other and serves as a substitute for him. They are the guardian angels according to the statement of most commentators.

Al-Zajjaj said: the mu'aqqibat are angels who come one after another in succession. He said "mu'aqqibat" even though the angels are male, because a group of angels is called mu'aqqibah, and then mu'aqqibah was made plural as mu'aqqibat. This meaning was mentioned by al-Farra'. It was also said: it is feminine because of the large number of them, like nassabah (great genealogist) and 'allamah (great scholar).

Al-Jawhari said: al-ta'aqqub means returning after the beginning.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He turned and fled without looking back﴾ [al-Naml: 10; al-Qasas: 31]. And it was recited ma'aqib, the plural of mu'qib.

﴿From before him and behind him﴾, that is, from before the one for whom the mu'aqqibat are, and the intended meaning is that the guardian angels are from all his sides. It was also said: the intended meaning of mu'aqqibat is the deeds, and the meaning of "from before him and from behind him" is what has preceded from them and what has come after.

﴿They protect him by the command of Allah﴾, that is, by the order of Allah.

It was also said: they protect him from the might of Allah when he sins, by granting him respite and seeking forgiveness for him until he repents.

Al-Farra' said: regarding this there are two views. One is that it is in inverted order (taqdim wa ta'khir), its meaning being: "For him there are mu'aqqibat by the command of Allah, protecting him from before him and from behind him." The second is that the protective act of the guardians is itself something Allah commanded.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that their protecting him is by the command of Allah, i.e., by what He commanded them, not that they have the power to repel Allah's command.

Ibn al-Anbari said: there is another view in this regard, namely that min (from) here means bi (by), i.e., "they protect him by the command of Allah." It was also said that min means 'an (from), i.e., "they protect him from the command of Allah," in the sense of "from the presence of Allah," not from their own presence, like His saying: ﴿He fed them against hunger﴾ [Quraysh: 4], i.e., against hunger. It was also said: they protect him from the angels of punishment. It was also said: they protect him from the jinn.

Ibn Jarir chose that the mu'aqqibat are the processions before rulers.

The meaning is that this does not repel the decree.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people﴾, of blessing and well-being, ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾, of obedience to Allah.

(p. 722; p. 723)

The meaning is that He does not take away a blessing He has bestowed on a people until they change what is within themselves of goodness and righteous deeds, or change the natural disposition (*fitrah*, the innate human nature) in which Allah created them.

It has been said: the intended meaning is not that He never sends a punishment upon any of His servants unless a sin has preceded it from that person. Rather, calamities may befall people because of the sins of others, as in the hadith that a questioner asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "Will we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us?" He said, "Yes, when corruption becomes widespread." ﴿And when Allah wills harm for a people﴾, that is, destruction and punishment, ﴿there is no turning it back﴾, that is, there is no one to repel it. It has also been said that the meaning is: when Allah wills harm for a people, He blinds their hearts until they choose that which brings affliction upon them. ﴿And they have no protector besides Him﴾ who would take charge of their affairs and whom they could seek refuge with, so that he might ward off from them the punishment that comes to them from Allah, the Glorified, or no helper who would aid them and prevent them from the punishment of Allah.

The meaning is: there is no one who can repel the punishment of Allah, nor anyone who can annul His judgment.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿And if you marvel, then marvelous is their saying﴾: he said, "If you marvel, O Muhammad, at their denial of you, then marvelous is their saying."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning the verse, he said: "If you marvel, O Muhammad, at their denial, though they have seen the power and command of Allah, and the parables He has set forth for them, and what He has shown them of the giving of life to the dead and to the dead earth ﴿then marvelous is their saying: 'When we have become dust, will we truly be in a new creation?'﴾ Do they not see that He created them from a drop of semen? Creating from a drop of semen is greater than creating from dust and bones."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿And exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾: he said, "The punishments."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah concerning the *mathulat* (exemplary punishments): he said, "They are the events of Allah among the nations concerning those who passed before you."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The *mathulat* are the punishments that befell the earlier generations."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing, and indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Were it not for the pardon of Allah and His overlooking, no one would enjoy a pleasant life; and were it not for His warning and His punishment, everyone would become complacent.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and for every people there is a guide﴾: he said, "A caller."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people a guide﴾: he said, "The warner is Muhammad (ﷺ), and ﴿for every people a guide﴾ is a prophet who calls them to Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "Muhammad is the warner, and the guide is Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid something similar as well.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the warner and he is the guide."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah and Abu al-Duha something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah*, al-Daylami, Ibn Asakir and Ibn al-Najjar narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people a guide﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed his hand upon his chest and said, 'I am the warner,' and he gestured with his hand toward the shoulder of Ali and said, 'You are the guide, O Ali; through you will be guided those who are guided after me.'" Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "This hadith contains severe objectionable content."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Barzah al-Aslami, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in *al-Mukhtarah* narrated from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well.

Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Musnad*, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning the verse something similar as well.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾: he said, "Every female among the creatures of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning the verse: he said, "He knows whether it is male or female." ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "It is the woman who sees blood during her pregnancy."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "The flow of blood." ﴿And what they increase﴾: he said, "Its retention."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "That she sees blood during her pregnancy." ﴿And what they increase﴾: he said, "In nine months." Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated through the route of al-Dahhak from him concerning the verse, he said: "What they increase beyond nine, and what they lose of the nine."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him concerning the verse ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "The miscarriage." ﴿And what they increase﴾: "What they add to the pregnancy beyond what they lost, until they give birth to it complete."

This is because among women there is one who carries for ten months, and among them one who carries for nine months, and among them one whose pregnancy is shorter.

So that is the diminishing and the increasing that Allah mentioned, and Allah, the Exalted, knows all of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning His words ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾: he said, "The secret and the public."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated concerning His words ﴿And whoever hides his speech at night or goes forth by day﴾: he said, "One who rides his head into sins." ﴿And one who goes forth freely by day﴾: he said, "One who openly commits sins by day."

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, ﴿and one who goes forth freely by day﴾: he said, "The open one." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "He is a person of suspicion who hides at night, and when he goes out by day he makes people think he is free of sin."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Kabir*, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il* narrated through the route of Ata' ibn Yasar from Ibn Abbas that the occasion of revelation of the verse was the arrival of Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Qays before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the well-known account, and that when Amir ibn al-Tufayl was afflicted with the plague (*ghuddah*), the words of Allah, the Exalted, were revealed: ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾ up to His words ﴿with angels following one another before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah﴾. He said: "The ones following one another by the command of Allah guard Muhammad (ﷺ)." Then he mentioned Arbad ibn Qays and what killed him, and He said: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾ up to His words ﴿and He is mighty in strength﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿with angels following one another﴾, the verse, he said: "This is specifically for the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿guarding him by the command of Allah﴾, he said: "That guarding is by the command of Allah, by the command of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him ﴿by the command of Allah﴾, he said: "By the permission of Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning the verse, he said: "The ruler's close attendants, who have guards around him, guarding him from before him and behind him." He means: they guard him from My command; for when I will harm a people, there is no turning it back.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "Kings take guards who protect him from in front of him, behind him, to his right and to his left, guarding him from being killed. Have you not heard that Allah says: ﴿But when Allah wills harm for a people, there is no turning it back﴾? That is, if He wills harm, the guards will not avail him anything."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah concerning the verse, he said: "These are the commanders."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They are the angels who follow one another by night, writing down about the son of Adam."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "Angels who guard him from before him and behind him; when the decree of Allah comes, they leave him alone."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ali concerning the verse, he said: "There is no servant except that with him are angels who guard him from a wall falling upon him, or from falling into a well, or from being eaten by a predator, or from drowning or burning. When the decree comes, they leave between him and the decree." Numerous hadiths have been transmitted concerning the mention of the guardians (*hafazah*) assigned to a human being, mentioned in the books of hadith.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 13, verses 5–11 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying﴾. That is, if you are amazed, O Muhammad, at their denial of you after you were among them as one known for truthfulness, then more amazing is their denial of the Resurrection.

Allah, exalted is He, cannot be described as being amazed (ta'ajjub), because amazement is a change in the soul caused by something whose causes are hidden. He mentioned it so that His Messenger and his followers would be amazed by it.

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, this matter is also astonishing, that they deny the Resurrection, while He has shown them, through the creation of the heavens and the earth, what proves that resurrection is easier in terms of power. It was also said: the verse concerns those who deny the Creator. That is, if you are amazed at their denial of the Creator despite the clear proofs that what changes must have a changer, then that is the object of amazement. But the first interpretation is preferable because of His saying: ﴿When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ This sentence is in the place of nominative case (raf') as a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitution) for their saying. It is permissible for it to be in the place of accusative case (nasb) as the object of the verb "said" (maqul al-qawl). According to the first view, the amazement refers to their own speech; according to the second, it refers to their speaking that way. The governing element of idha ("when") is what is implied by His saying ﴿Will we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, which is "we will be raised" or "we will be returned."

Their question is one of denial, which expresses the utmost remoteness of the idea. The fronting of the adverbial phrase in His saying ﴿in a new creation﴾ emphasizes the denial of resurrection. Likewise, the repetition of the hamza (interrogative particle) in His saying: a'idha (ʾa-ʾinnā), i.e., ﴿Are we…? Are we…?﴾

Then, when Allah, glorified is He, related that about them, He passed judgment on them concerning three matters. The first: ﴿They are those who disbelieved in their Lord﴾. That is, those who deny His power to resurrect are those who persist in disbelief and are complete in it.

The second: ﴿And they will have shackles around their necks﴾. Al-aghlal (shackles) is the plural of ghull, which is a collar by which the hand is tied to the neck. That is, they will be shackled with them on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the shackles are their evil deeds, which cling to them as collars cling to necks.

The third: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾, never leaving it under any circumstances. The placement of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) indicates that eternal abiding is specific to those who deny the Resurrection.

﴿And they ask you to hasten evil before good﴾. The evil (al-sayyi'ah) is the destroying punishment. The good (al-hasanah) is well-being and safety. They said this statement out of their extreme denial, their intense resolve, and their obsession with disbelief. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is that they requested punishment before good, which is faith.

﴿And there have already occurred before them the exemplary punishments (al-mathulat)﴾. The majority of readers recited mathulat with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the thaʾ, the plural of mathulah, like samurah, which means punishment. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-mathulah is a punishment that leaves a blemish on the one punished by altering some part of his form, from the saying: "Fulan mutilated Fulan" when he disfigured his body by cutting off his nose, gouging out his eyes, or ripping open his belly.

Al-A'mash recited it with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the thaʾ, for lightness, since the damma is heavy. In the dialect of Tamim it is with a damma on both the mim and the thaʾ. Its singular in their dialect is muthlah, with a damma on the mim and a sukun on the thaʾ, like ghurfah and ghurufat.

It is also reported from al-A'mash in another narration that he recited this word with a damma on it, according to the dialect of Tamim.

The meaning: these people ask you to hasten the sending of punishment upon them, although punishments of their like among the deniers have already passed before them. So why do they not take warning from them and beware of what befell those others? The sentence is in the place of accusative case as a circumstantial clause (hal). This hastening by these people is in the manner of mockery, like their saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You…﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], to the end of the verse.

﴿And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness﴾, that is, full of great pardon, ﴿toward people despite their wrongdoing﴾ against themselves by committing sins and falling into disobedience, if they repent from that and return to Allah, glorified is He. The prepositional phrase, i.e., "despite their wrongdoing," is in the place of accusative case as a circumstantial clause, meaning while they are wrongdoers. The particle ʿalā here has the meaning of maʿa ("with"), i.e., "with their wrongdoing." In the verse there is a great glad tiding and a great hope, because it is known that a person while engaged in wrongdoing is not repentant. For this reason it was said that it refers specifically to the sinners among the monotheists. It was also said: the forgiveness mentioned here means the delay of punishment until the Hereafter, to match what Allah related of the disbelievers' hastening for punishment, as the sentence mentioned after this verse indicates, namely: ﴿And indeed, your Lord is severe in punishment﴾, He punishes the disobedient deniers among the disbelievers with severe punishment in the Hereafter, according to what His will requires.

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ That is, why has a sign other than what he has already brought of the signs not been sent down upon him? These disbelievers who make this statement are the ones who hasten for the punishment.

Al-Zajjaj said: They requested signs other than those he had brought, so they sought the like of the signs of Moses and Jesus. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿You are only a warner﴾, warning them of the Fire, and no sign is in your hands. End of quote.

This is arrogance and obstinacy on the part of the disbelievers, since Allah had indeed sent down to His Messenger signs sufficient for those who are guided. The phrase ﴿You are only a warner﴾ comes in the form of restriction (hasr) to show that he, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, is a messenger for warning the servants and for explaining what they should beware of as its consequence, and that there is nothing else incumbent upon him beyond that.

He has done what is incumbent upon him: he warned with the most eloquent warning, and he left nothing by which that warning is achieved without bringing it, clarifying it, and repeating it.

May Allah reward him on behalf of his community with goodness.

﴿And for every people is a guide﴾, that is, a prophet who calls them to what contains their guidance and right direction, even if guidance does not actually reach them and they do not accept it. The signs of the messengers differ: one brings a sign or signs that another did not bring, according to what Allah gives of them. Whoever demands from some of them what another brought has reached an enormous level of obstinacy. Therefore, the purpose of signs is only to indicate prophethood, since they are miracles beyond human capacity, and that does not restrict to any single one of them, nor to specific individuals.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿And for every people is a guide﴾ is that the guide is Allah, mighty and majestic is He, for He is capable of that, and upon His prophets is only the mere warning.

﴿Allah knows what every female carries﴾. This sentence is resumptive (mustanʾafah), brought to show His comprehensive knowledge, glorified is He, and His knowledge of the unseen of which these matters mentioned are part.

It was said: it is also permissible that the noble name (Allah) is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "And for every people is a guide, and he is Allah." The sentence ﴿knows what every female carries﴾ would then be an explanation of "guide" according to the last view. But this is very far-fetched. Here, "mā" (what) is a relative pronoun, meaning: He knows that which every female carries in her womb, whether a clot, or a lump of flesh, or male or female, or beautiful or ugly, or fortunate or wretched.

It is also permissible that it be an interrogative (istifhamiyyah), meaning: He knows what thing is in her womb and in what state it is.

It is also permissible that it be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), meaning: He knows her carrying.

﴿And what the wombs decrease and what they increase﴾. Al-ghayd means decrease. That is, He knows what the wombs decrease, i.e., diminish, and He knows what they increase.

It was said: the intended meaning is the decrease in the formation of the fetus and its increase, such as the decrease of a finger or its increase. It was said: the intended meaning is the decrease in the duration of pregnancy below nine months, or its increase. It was said: if a woman menstruates while pregnant, that is a decrease in her child. It was said: al-ghayd is what the wombs diminish of blood, and the increase is what they add to it. The particle mā in "what they decrease and what they increase" admits the three possibilities mentioned earlier concerning "what every female carries."

﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾, that is, everything among the things of which those mentioned are part is with Allah, glorified is He, in measure. Measure (miqdar) is the extent that Allah has ordained. This is the meaning of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, all things We have created in measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49], that is, all things with Allah, glorified is He, proceed according to His decree which has already preceded and been finished, and nothing departs from that.

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, that is, Knower of everything absent from the senses and everything present and witnessed, or Knower of everything nonexistent and existent. There is no obstacle to interpreting the statement as including what is more general than that.

﴿The Great, the Most High﴾, that is, the Magnificent, before whom everything is lesser, the Exalted above what the polytheists say, or the One who is高 above everything by His power, majesty, and dominion.

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned that He knows those unseen matters, none of which escapes Him, He explained that He knows what they conceal within themselves and what they proclaim to others, and that this is not different to Him. So He said: ﴿Whether one of you conceals speech or openly speaks it﴾. So He knows what a person conceals just as He knows what he openly does, whether good or evil.

His saying "among you" (minkum) is connected to "equal" (sawa'), meaning: "the one who conceals and the one who openly declares are equal among you," or "the secret of the one who conceals and the open speech of the one who speaks openly."

﴿And whoever is hidden by night﴾, that is, concealed in the darkness that exists at night, hiding from eyes. It is said: "the thing was hidden" (khafiya) and "he hid himself" (istakhfa), meaning he concealed himself and hid. ﴿And one who goes freely by day﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: sariba yasrubu sarban and suruban means he went away, and from this is the poet's saying:

Every people has gathered around the tether of its stallion, but we have loosed its tether, so it is free to go.

That is, it went away.

Al-Qutaybi said: sarib by day means one who moves about freely in his needs with speed, from the saying "the water flowed away" (asraba al-ma').

Al-Asma'i said: sarabuhu means his path or way.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: the one who is openly manifest in speech, the one who conceals in his soul, the one who appears in the roads, and the one who hides in the darkness are all equally known to Allah. This is closest to the meaning of the verse, as the contrast between "the one who hides" and "the one who goes freely" indicates: the one who hides is the one concealed, and the one who goes freely is the one who is manifest and visible.

﴿For him there are successive (mu'aqqibat) [angels]﴾. The pronoun in "for him" refers to "whoever" in His saying: ﴿whether one of you conceals speech or openly speaks it, and whoever is hidden﴾. That is, for each of these there are mu'aqqibat. The mu'aqqibat are those who alternate, each of whom succeeds the other and serves as a substitute for him. They are the guardian angels according to the statement of most commentators.

Al-Zajjaj said: the mu'aqqibat are angels who come one after another in succession. He said "mu'aqqibat" even though the angels are male, because a group of angels is called mu'aqqibah, and then mu'aqqibah was made plural as mu'aqqibat. This meaning was mentioned by al-Farra'. It was also said: it is feminine because of the large number of them, like nassabah (great genealogist) and 'allamah (great scholar).

Al-Jawhari said: al-ta'aqqub means returning after the beginning.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He turned and fled without looking back﴾ [al-Naml: 10; al-Qasas: 31]. And it was recited ma'aqib, the plural of mu'qib.

﴿From before him and behind him﴾, that is, from before the one for whom the mu'aqqibat are, and the intended meaning is that the guardian angels are from all his sides. It was also said: the intended meaning of mu'aqqibat is the deeds, and the meaning of "from before him and from behind him" is what has preceded from them and what has come after.

﴿They protect him by the command of Allah﴾, that is, by the order of Allah.

It was also said: they protect him from the might of Allah when he sins, by granting him respite and seeking forgiveness for him until he repents.

Al-Farra' said: regarding this there are two views. One is that it is in inverted order (taqdim wa ta'khir), its meaning being: "For him there are mu'aqqibat by the command of Allah, protecting him from before him and from behind him." The second is that the protective act of the guardians is itself something Allah commanded.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that their protecting him is by the command of Allah, i.e., by what He commanded them, not that they have the power to repel Allah's command.

Ibn al-Anbari said: there is another view in this regard, namely that min (from) here means bi (by), i.e., "they protect him by the command of Allah." It was also said that min means 'an (from), i.e., "they protect him from the command of Allah," in the sense of "from the presence of Allah," not from their own presence, like His saying: ﴿He fed them against hunger﴾ [Quraysh: 4], i.e., against hunger. It was also said: they protect him from the angels of punishment. It was also said: they protect him from the jinn.

Ibn Jarir chose that the mu'aqqibat are the processions before rulers.

The meaning is that this does not repel the decree.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people﴾, of blessing and well-being, ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾, of obedience to Allah.

(p. 722; p. 723)

The meaning is that He does not take away a blessing He has bestowed on a people until they change what is within themselves of goodness and righteous deeds, or change the natural disposition (*fitrah*, the innate human nature) in which Allah created them.

It has been said: the intended meaning is not that He never sends a punishment upon any of His servants unless a sin has preceded it from that person. Rather, calamities may befall people because of the sins of others, as in the hadith that a questioner asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "Will we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us?" He said, "Yes, when corruption becomes widespread." ﴿And when Allah wills harm for a people﴾, that is, destruction and punishment, ﴿there is no turning it back﴾, that is, there is no one to repel it. It has also been said that the meaning is: when Allah wills harm for a people, He blinds their hearts until they choose that which brings affliction upon them. ﴿And they have no protector besides Him﴾ who would take charge of their affairs and whom they could seek refuge with, so that he might ward off from them the punishment that comes to them from Allah, the Glorified, or no helper who would aid them and prevent them from the punishment of Allah.

The meaning is: there is no one who can repel the punishment of Allah, nor anyone who can annul His judgment.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿And if you marvel, then marvelous is their saying﴾: he said, "If you marvel, O Muhammad, at their denial of you, then marvelous is their saying."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning the verse, he said: "If you marvel, O Muhammad, at their denial, though they have seen the power and command of Allah, and the parables He has set forth for them, and what He has shown them of the giving of life to the dead and to the dead earth ﴿then marvelous is their saying: 'When we have become dust, will we truly be in a new creation?'﴾ Do they not see that He created them from a drop of semen? Creating from a drop of semen is greater than creating from dust and bones."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿And exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾: he said, "The punishments."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah concerning the *mathulat* (exemplary punishments): he said, "They are the events of Allah among the nations concerning those who passed before you."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The *mathulat* are the punishments that befell the earlier generations."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing, and indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Were it not for the pardon of Allah and His overlooking, no one would enjoy a pleasant life; and were it not for His warning and His punishment, everyone would become complacent.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and for every people there is a guide﴾: he said, "A caller."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people a guide﴾: he said, "The warner is Muhammad (ﷺ), and ﴿for every people a guide﴾ is a prophet who calls them to Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "Muhammad is the warner, and the guide is Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid something similar as well.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the warner and he is the guide."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah and Abu al-Duha something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah*, al-Daylami, Ibn Asakir and Ibn al-Najjar narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people a guide﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed his hand upon his chest and said, 'I am the warner,' and he gestured with his hand toward the shoulder of Ali and said, 'You are the guide, O Ali; through you will be guided those who are guided after me.'" Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "This hadith contains severe objectionable content."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Barzah al-Aslami, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in *al-Mukhtarah* narrated from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well.

Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Musnad*, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning the verse something similar as well.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾: he said, "Every female among the creatures of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning the verse: he said, "He knows whether it is male or female." ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "It is the woman who sees blood during her pregnancy."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "The flow of blood." ﴿And what they increase﴾: he said, "Its retention."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "That she sees blood during her pregnancy." ﴿And what they increase﴾: he said, "In nine months." Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated through the route of al-Dahhak from him concerning the verse, he said: "What they increase beyond nine, and what they lose of the nine."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him concerning the verse ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾: he said, "The miscarriage." ﴿And what they increase﴾: "What they add to the pregnancy beyond what they lost, until they give birth to it complete."

This is because among women there is one who carries for ten months, and among them one who carries for nine months, and among them one whose pregnancy is shorter.

So that is the diminishing and the increasing that Allah mentioned, and Allah, the Exalted, knows all of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning His words ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾: he said, "The secret and the public."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated concerning His words ﴿And whoever hides his speech at night or goes forth by day﴾: he said, "One who rides his head into sins." ﴿And one who goes forth freely by day﴾: he said, "One who openly commits sins by day."

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, ﴿and one who goes forth freely by day﴾: he said, "The open one." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "He is a person of suspicion who hides at night, and when he goes out by day he makes people think he is free of sin."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Kabir*, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il* narrated through the route of Ata' ibn Yasar from Ibn Abbas that the occasion of revelation of the verse was the arrival of Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Qays before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the well-known account, and that when Amir ibn al-Tufayl was afflicted with the plague (*ghuddah*), the words of Allah, the Exalted, were revealed: ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾ up to His words ﴿with angels following one another before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah﴾. He said: "The ones following one another by the command of Allah guard Muhammad (ﷺ)." Then he mentioned Arbad ibn Qays and what killed him, and He said: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾ up to His words ﴿and He is mighty in strength﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿with angels following one another﴾, the verse, he said: "This is specifically for the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿guarding him by the command of Allah﴾, he said: "That guarding is by the command of Allah, by the command of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him ﴿by the command of Allah﴾, he said: "By the permission of Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning the verse, he said: "The ruler's close attendants, who have guards around him, guarding him from before him and behind him." He means: they guard him from My command; for when I will harm a people, there is no turning it back.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "Kings take guards who protect him from in front of him, behind him, to his right and to his left, guarding him from being killed. Have you not heard that Allah says: ﴿But when Allah wills harm for a people, there is no turning it back﴾? That is, if He wills harm, the guards will not avail him anything."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah concerning the verse, he said: "These are the commanders."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They are the angels who follow one another by night, writing down about the son of Adam."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: "Angels who guard him from before him and behind him; when the decree of Allah comes, they leave him alone."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ali concerning the verse, he said: "There is no servant except that with him are angels who guard him from a wall falling upon him, or from falling into a well, or from being eaten by a predator, or from drowning or burning. When the decree comes, they leave between him and the decree." Numerous hadiths have been transmitted concerning the mention of the guardians (*hafazah*) assigned to a human being, mentioned in the books of hadith.

When He, glory be to Him, frightened His servants with the sending down of what cannot be averted, He followed it with matters that in some respects give hope and in others cause fear: lightning, clouds, thunder, and thunderbolt. The meanings of these words and their causes were explained at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

There is disagreement about the grammatical status of ﴿khawfan wa-ṭamaʿan﴾ ("in fear and in hope"). It has been said that it is an absolute object (maṣdar, a verbal noun used as an accusative of cognate meaning), i.e., "so that you fear and so that you hope, a hope." It has been said that it is an accusative of purpose (ʿillah), on the assumption of the intention of fear and hope, so that the subject of the causative verb and the subject of the object of purpose do not differ. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring to the lightning, or to the addressees, with the sense "people who are fearful." Other views have been held that have no need to be mentioned.

It has been said: the fear is that which arises from the thunderbolts, and the hope is that which arises from the rain.

Al-Zajjāj said: the fear is for the traveller, because of what harms him from the rain, and the hope is for the resident, because when he sees the lightning he hopes for the rain, which is the cause of fertility.

﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾: the definite article here is generic (li-l-jins), and the singular is saḥābah (a cloud). "Thiqāl" is the plural of thaqīlah (heavy).

The meaning is that God, glory be to Him, makes the clouds that He produces heavy by the water He places in them.

﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾: that is, the thunder itself glorifies God with the praise of God, meaning in a state of being joined with His praise. This is not improbable, and there is nothing to prevent God from causing it to speak thus: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 44].

As for interpreting "the thunder" as an angel among the angels, there is no improbability in that either. Its mention in the singular, followed by the mention of the angels after it, would be for additional distinction and special care. It has been said that the meaning is: the hearers of the thunder glorify, that is, they say, "Glory be to God and praise be to God." ﴿And the angels, out of fear of Him﴾: that is, the angels glorify out of fear of God, glory be to Him. It has been said: out of fear of the thunder.

A group of exegetes have mentioned that these angels are the helpers of the thunder, and that God, glory be to Him, made for it helpers.

﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾ among His creatures, so that He destroys him. The context of these matters here serves the purpose for which the preceding verses were brought, which is the demonstration of the perfection of His power.

﴿Yet they dispute concerning God﴾: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers addressed in His saying "It is He who shows you the lightning." That is: these disbelievers, despite these signs which God showed them, dispute concerning the affair of God, glory be to Him. They deny the resurrection at one time, and at another they seek to hasten the punishment; they deny the messengers and disobey God. This clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it is permissible that it be a resumed (istiʾnāfiyyah) clause.

﴿And He is severe in might (miḥāl)﴾: Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: al-miḥāl is cunning, and cunning from God is planning with truth.

Al-Naḥḥās said: cunning from God is bringing harm upon the one who deserves it from a direction he does not perceive.

Al-Azharī said: al-miḥāl is strength and vehemence, and the letter mīm is original (not augmentative); one says māḥaltu fulānan miḥālan, "whichever of us is stronger."

Abū ʿUbayd said: al-miḥāl is punishment and harm.

Al-Zajjāj said: one says māḥaltuhu miḥālan when you contend with him until it becomes clear which of you is stronger, and al-maḥl in the language means vehemence.

Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, severe in guile. Its origin is from stratagem, and the mīm was made like the mīm of place (mafʿal); its origin is from being established (al-kawn), then one says tamakkantu.

Al-Azharī said: Ibn Qutaybah erred in claiming that the mīm in it is augmentative; rather it is original. Whenever you see a word in the pattern fiʿāl whose first letter is a kasrah-vowelled mīm, it is original, like mihād, milāk, and mirās, and other such words.

Al-Aʿraj read ﴿and He is severe in might﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm (maḥāl). This reading has been interpreted as meaning "power" (ḥawl).

Among the Companions and the Successors there are eight opinions on the interpretation of al-miḥāl here: the first is enmity; the second is power (ḥawl); the third is seizing; the fourth is rancour; the fifth is strength; the sixth is anger; the seventh is destruction; the eighth is stratagem.

﴿To Him is the call of truth (daʿwat al-ḥaqq)﴾: the attribution of the call to truth is an attribution of association: that is, the call that is associated with truth, specific to Him, into which falsehood has no entry in any way, just as one says "the word of truth." The meaning is that it is an answered call, fulfilled in its proper place, unlike the call of those other than Him.

It has been said: the truth is God, glory be to Him, and the meaning is that for God, glory be to Him, is the call of the One who is truly called, who hears and responds.

It has been said: the intended meaning of the call of truth here is the word of monotheism and sincerity, and the meaning is: for God, from among His creatures, is that they should affirm His oneness and be sincere to Him.

It has been said: the call of truth is calling upon Him, glory be to Him, at the time of fear, for no one else is called upon at that time, as He said: ﴿Those whom you call upon fall away, except Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 67].

It has been said: the call is worship, for the worship of God is the truth and the reality.

﴿And those who call upon others besides Him do not respond to them with anything﴾: that is, the gods whom the disbelievers call upon besides God, mighty and majestic, do not respond to them with anything of what they ask of them, whatever it may be, except a response like the response of water to one who spreads his palms toward it from afar. For it does not respond to him, because it is inanimate and does not perceive his need for it, nor does it know that he asked it to reach his mouth. Hence He said: ﴿nor is it (the water) reaching him﴾, that is, the water does not reach into him.

Al-Zajjāj said: it is like the response given to one who spreads his palms toward water, calling the water to his mouth, and the water does not respond. God, glory be to Him, informed them that their calling upon the idols is like the calling of a thirsty man upon water, asking it to reach his mouth, and the water does not reach it.

It has been said: the meaning is that he is like one who spreads his hands toward water in order to grasp it, but nothing of it attains his palm. The Arabs have struck the proverb of grasping water for one who strives after what he cannot attain, as the poet said:

"So I became, from what was between me and her of affection, like one who grasps water in his hand."

And another said:

"Whoever trusts in this world becomes like one who grasps water, whose hand is betrayed by the gaps between his fingers."

Al-Farrāʾ said: the water here is the water of a well, because the well is a source of water. He likened the one who extends his hand to the well without a rope to one who calls upon others among the idols. God, glory be to Him, struck this as a parable for one who calls upon other than Him.

﴿And the call of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾: that is, that call goes astray from them, so they find nothing from it, and it benefits them in no way at all; rather it is lost and gone.

﴿And to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾: If by prostration is meant its literal meaning, which is placing the forehead on the ground in glorification with humility and submission, then this is evident regarding the believers, the angels, and the Muslim jinn. As for the disbelievers, it is not valid to interpret prostration in this sense concerning them. Therefore prostration mentioned in the verse must be understood in the sense that prostration is due to God and is required, so that it includes prostration in deed and other than it; or prostration is interpreted as submission, for the disbelievers, although they do not prostrate to God, glory be to Him, are nonetheless subject to His command and judgement regarding them in health and sickness, life and death, poverty and wealth. What confirms this meaning is His saying: ﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾, for the disbelievers submit unwillingly as the believers submit willingly. Both are in the accusative as maṣdar (verbal noun): that is, submission of willingness and submission of unwillingness; or as circumstantial accusatives: willing and unwilling.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the verse is specific to the believers, for they prostrate willingly, while some disbelievers prostrate under compulsion and fear, like the hypocrites; so the verse is understood as referring to these. It has been said: the verse refers to the believers, among whom some prostrate willingly, for whom prostration is not burdensome, and some for whom it is burdensome, because accepting the obligation is a hardship; but they bear the hardship out of faith in God and sincerity to Him.

﴿And their shadows, in the mornings and the evenings﴾: "shadows" is the plural of shadow (ẓill), and what is meant by it is the shadow of a person that follows him. It is made to prostrate by his prostration, since it becomes inseparable from him and never leaves him.

Al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Anbārī said: it is not unlikely that God creates for the shadows understandings by which they prostrate to God, glory be to Him, just as He gave understanding to the mountains so that they were occupied with His glorification. Thus the shadow of the believer prostrates to God willingly, and the shadow of the disbeliever prostrates to God unwillingly.

The mornings and evenings are singled out for mention because the shadows become most apparent at these two times. They are the time-adverb for the implied prostration: that is, their shadows prostrate at these two times.

The interpretation of "mornings and evenings" has been mentioned in al-Aʿrāf. Among what has the same meaning as this verse is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Have they not seen that whatever thing God has created, its shadows incline from right and left, prostrating to God, and they are humbled?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 48].

He used "man" (who) in ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ by way of giving precedence to rational beings over others, and because the prostration of others is a consequence of their prostration. Among what supports understanding prostration as submission is that the placing of "to God" before the verb conveys exclusivity, for the prostration of the disbelievers to their idols is well known, and they do not submit to them in the way they submit to God in matters which they themselves acknowledge to be from God, such as creation, life, death, and the like.

﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?﴾ God, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger to ask the disbelievers: who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Then, since they were acknowledging this and confessing it, as God, glory be to Him, related in His saying: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: they were created by the Mighty, the Knowing﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9], and His saying ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say: God﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87], He commanded His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to answer, so He said: ﴿Say: God﴾. It is as if He related their answer and what they believe, because they might falter in answering out of fear of what would be binding on them. Then He commanded him to impose the proof upon them and confound them, so He said: ﴿Say: Have you then taken, besides Him, protectors?﴾ The interrogative is for denial: that is, if the Lord of the heavens and the earth is God, as you acknowledge and confess, as He related about you in His saying: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne? They will say: God﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 86–87].

Then how is it that you have taken for yourselves, besides Him, protectors who are powerless, ﴿who possess no benefit for themselves﴾, bringing benefit to themselves by it, ﴿nor harm﴾, causing harm to others by it or warding off harm from themselves? So how do you hope for benefit and harm from them when they do not possess either for themselves? The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

Then God, glory be to Him, struck a parable for them and commanded His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say it to them. So He said: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ That is: is the blind man in his religion, who is the disbeliever, equal to the seeing man in it, who is the monotheist? For the former is ignorant of what is obligatory for him and what is binding on him, while the latter knows that.

Ibn Muḥayṣin, Abū Bakr, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "Or are the darkness and the light equal?" with the yāʾ (third person), and the rest read it with the tāʾ (second person). Abū ʿUbayd preferred the second reading.

The darkness refers to disbelief, and the light to faith. The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach: that is, how can they be equal when between them there is the same disparity as between the blind and the seeing, and between darkness and light? The light is in the singular and the darkness in the plural, because the path of truth is one and does not differ, while the paths of falsehood are many and not limited.

﴿Or have they set up for God partners who created as He created, so that the creation seemed alike to them?﴾ The particle "am" here is the disjunctive one, which means "rather" together with the hamzah: that is, rather, have they made for God partners who created as He created? The interrogative is for denying that this has occurred.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: its meaning is: have they made for God partners who created the like of what God created, so that the creation of the partners became similar to the creation of God in their view? That is, the matter is not so, that the affair should be confused for them; rather, if they reflect with their minds, they will find that God is the one alone who creates, while the rest of the partners create nothing. The clause ﴿who created as He created﴾ is in the accusative position as a descriptive clause of "partners."

The meaning is: they did not set up partners for God who share in creating as He creates, so that "the creation" would be confused for them by this cause, and so deserve worship from them. Rather, they set up idols and the like as partners to Him, and those are far from being like that. Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to make the truth clear to them and guide them to what is right, so He said: ﴿Say: "God is the Creator of all things,"﴾ whatever they may be, and no one else has any share in that in any way whatsoever.

Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and Qur'an exegete) said: The meaning is that He is the Creator of everything that can be created. Do you not see that He, exalted is He, is a "thing" but is not created? ﴿And He is the One,﴾ that is, the Sole in lordship, the Subduer over everything besides Him. So everything other than Him is a subject, subdued and overcome.

Then God, glorified is He, struck another parable for the truth and its adherents, and for falsehood and its claimants. He said: ﴿He sends down water from the sky,﴾ that is, from its direction. The indefiniteness of "water" (māʾan) is for abundance or for kind. ﴿So valleys flow according to their measure﴾ (awdiyah, plural of wādī, which is any open space between two mountains or the like).

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi (a grammarian) said: We know of no active participle (fāʿil) pluralized on the pattern afʿilah except this one. It seems it was treated as if it were on the pattern faʿīl, and so pluralized as afʿilah, like jarīb and ajribah. Just as faʿīl was treated as fāʿil and so pluralized as afʿāl, like yatīm and aytām, sharīf and ashrāf, and as aṣḥāb and anṣār for ṣāḥib and nāṣir. He said: In His words ﴿so valleys flow﴾ there is a figurative expression (tawassuʿ), meaning: its water flowed. He said: The meaning of "according to their measure" is according to the measure of their water, because the valleys did not flow by their own measure.

Al-Wahidi said: The qadar (measure) is the extent of a thing. The meaning: according to their measure of water. If the valley is small, little water flows; if it is wide, much water flows. In al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) it says: "according to their measure" means according to the amount which God knows to be beneficial to those on whom it rains and not harmful. Ibn al-Anbari said: The descent of the Qur'an, which gathers guidance and clarity, is likened to the descent of rain, since the benefit of the Qur'an's descent is general, as the benefit of rain's descent is general. The valleys are likened to hearts, since water settles in valleys as the Qur'an and faith settle in the hearts of believers. ﴿So the torrent carried a swelling foam.﴾ Zabad (foam) is the white, raised, puffed-up thing on the surface of the torrent, also called ghuthāʾ (scum) and rughwah (froth).
