Rābī (swelling) is what is high and raised above the water.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is what floats on the water. Others said: It is what increases because of its swelling, from rabā yarbū, meaning it increased.

What is meant by this is the likening of disbelief to the foam that rises on water: it vanishes, clings to the edges of the valley, and the winds drive it away. Likewise, disbelief departs and vanishes.

The first parable is complete. Then God, glorified is He, began to mention the second parable, so He said: ﴿And from what they heat in the fire﴾ (min, for the beginning of the extent: from it arises foam like the foam of water; or partitive: some of it is foam like it). The pronoun refers to humankind, left implicit because it is clear from context. This is according to the reading "yūqidūna" with the yāʾ (third person), which Ḥumayd, Ibn Muḥaysin, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ recited. The rest read it with the tāʾ (second person, address), and Abu ʿUbayd preferred the first reading.

The meaning: ﴿and from what you heat in the fire,﴾ so that what is molten of the substances that melt, ﴿seeking an ornament,﴾ that is, seeking to make ornaments with which you adorn and beautify yourselves, like gold and silver, ﴿or a commodity,﴾ that is, or seeking a commodity you enjoy, from vessels and tools made of iron, brass, copper, and lead, ﴿there is foam like it.﴾ The foam here means the dross, for it rises above what is melted of those substances, just as foam rises on water. So the pronoun in "like it" refers to ﴿a swelling foam﴾, and "foam" (zabad) is the subject, its predicate being ﴿from what they heat﴾.

﴿Thus God strikes the parables of truth and falsehood.﴾ That is, in the likeness of that wondrous striking, God strikes the parable of truth and the parable of falsehood. Then He began to divide the parable, so He said: ﴿As for the foam, it passes away as scum (jufāʾ).﴾ One says: "jafaʾa al-wādī" (with hamza) jufāʾan, when the valley casts out filth and foam.

Al-Farraʾ said: al-jufāʾ is the casting out. One says: the valley cast out its scum (ghuthāʾahu) as jufāʾ, when it threw it away. Jufāʾ is in the position of ghuthāʾ.

Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said the same. Abu ʿUbaydah related that he heard Ruʾbah recite "jufālan."

Abu ʿUbaydah said: One says "ajfalat al-qidr" when the pot casts out its foam, and "ajfalat al-rīḥ al-saḥāb" when the wind cuts through the clouds.

Abu Ḥātim said: Ruʾbah's reading is not to be recited, because he used to eat mice.

Know that the aspect of likeness between the two foams, in the foam that the torrent carries and the foam that rises on the heated substances, is that when the earth's dust mixed with the water and carried it along, it became a swelling foam above it. Likewise, what is heated in the fire until the melting substances melt: their origin is from the minerals that grow in the earth, and dust mixes with them. When they are melted, that dust which mixed with them becomes dross raised above them.

﴿As for what benefits people,﴾ from these two, which is the pure water and the pure molten substance free of dross, ﴿it remains in the earth,﴾ that is, it stays there. As for the water, it runs through the veins of the earth, and people benefit from it. As for what is melted of those substances, it is fashioned into ornaments and goods. These are two parables God struck for truth and falsehood. He says: falsehood, even if it appears over truth at times and rises above it, God, glorified is He, will surely erase it and annul it, and make the final outcome belong to the truth and its people. It is like the foam that rises on water, which the water casts away and which vanishes, and like the dross of those substances, which, though it rises over them, the furnace casts out and expels. This is the parable of falsehood. As for the water that benefits people and makes pastures grow, it remains in the earth. Likewise, the pure part of those substances remains pure, with no admixture. This is the parable of truth.

Al-Zajjaj said: The parable of the believer, his belief, and the benefit of faith is like the parable of this water which is used for the growth of the earth and the life of everything. It is also like the benefit of silver, gold, and all precious substances, for all of these remain as useful things. The parable of the disbeliever and his disbelief is like the foam which passes away as scum, and like the dross of iron and what the fire expels from the filth of silver and gold, which is of no use.

We have already related from Ibn al-Anbari, above, that he likened the descent of the Qur'an, and so on to the end of what we mentioned, and made that a parable God struck for the Qur'an. ﴿Thus God strikes parables,﴾ that is, in the likeness of that wondrous striking, God strikes parables in every matter, out of complete care for His servants and gentleness toward them. This is an emphasis on His words: ﴿Thus God strikes the truth and falsehood.﴾

Then God, glorified is He, explained who among His servants were the subjects of the parable of truth and the parable of falsehood. Regarding those for whom the parable of truth was struck, He said: ﴿For those who answered their Lord﴾ (that is, who responded to His call when He summoned them to His oneness, to affirm His messengers, and to act by His laws), ﴿is the best (al-ḥusnā)﴾, an adjective for an omitted noun: that is, the best reward, which is Paradise. Regarding those for whom the parable of falsehood was struck, He said: ﴿And those who did not answer Him﴾ (that is, His call to what He summoned them to), the relative clause is the subject, and its predicate is the conditional sentence: ﴿if they had all that is in the earth together﴾ of kinds of wealth which servants possess and gather, such that none of it would leave their ownership, ﴿and the like of it with it,﴾ that is, the like of all that is in the earth, existing alongside it and added to it, ﴿they would ransom themselves with it.﴾ That is, with all that was mentioned, which is what is in the earth and its like.

The meaning: to free themselves by it from the great punishment and the terrible horror they are in. Then God, glorified is He, explained what He had prepared for them, saying: ﴿Those, for them is the evil reckoning.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: Because their disbelief nullified their deeds. Others said: the evil reckoning is the strict scrutiny of it; and it was said: it is that a man is called to account for all his sin, and none of it is forgiven. ﴿Their abode is Hell,﴾ that is, their return is to it. ﴿And how wretched is the resting place,﴾ that is, the place where they settle.

The one singled out for blame is omitted.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as fear and hope﴾: He said: fear for the traveler, who fears its harm and hardship; and hope for the resident, who hopes for God's provision and hopes for the blessing and benefit of rain.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan who said: fear for the people of the sea, and hope for the people of the land.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak who said: the fear is what is feared from thunderbolts, and the hope is the rain.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Kharaʾiti in Makarim al-Akhlaq, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related through several chains from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib who said: Lightning is torches of fire in the hands of the angels of the clouds, with which they drive the clouds.

It is related from a group of the early generation what agrees with this and what contradicts it, and perhaps we have already mentioned some of that in Surat al-Baqarah.

Ahmad related from a shaykh of the Banu Ghifar who had accompanied the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "God creates the clouds, and they speak in the best speech, and laugh in the best laugh." It was said: the intended meaning of their speech is thunder, and of their laughter is lightning.

It is established with Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi in al-Yawm wa al-Layla, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard thunder and thunderbolts, he said: 'O God, do not kill us with Your wrath, do not destroy us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that.'"

Al-ʿUqayli related it and declared it weak, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God creates the clouds, then sends down water in them. There is nothing more beautiful than their laughter, nor more beautiful than their speech. Their speech is thunder and their laughter is lightning."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that Khuzaymah ibn Thabit, not the Ansari, "asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the origin of the clouds. He said: 'An angel assigned to them gathers the distant and joins the near, with a torch in his hand. When he raises it, it flashes; when he drives, it thunders; and when he strikes, it bursts (into thunderbolts).'"

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasaʾi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dalaʾil, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, we will ask you about five things. If you inform us of them, we will know you are a prophet and follow you.' He took from them the covenant that Israel took from his sons when he said: ﴿God is Witness over what we say.﴾ He said: 'Ask.' They said: 'Tell us about the sign of the prophet.' He said: 'His eyes sleep but his heart does not sleep.' They said: 'Tell us how a woman produces a female child and how a male child.' He said: 'The two waters meet; if the man's water rises above the woman's, a male is produced, and if the woman's water rises above the man's, a female is produced.' They said: 'Tell us what Israel forbade to himself.' He said: 'He suffered from sciatica, and found nothing that suited him except the milk of such-and-such,' meaning camels, 'so he forbade their meat.' They said: 'You have spoken truly.' They said: 'Tell us what this thunder is.' He said: 'An angel of God's angels assigned to the clouds, with a torch of fire in his hand, with which he drives the clouds wherever God commands him.' They said: 'Then what is this voice that we hear?' He said: 'Its voice.'"

They said: "You have spoken the truth. Only one remains, and it is the one we will follow you in if you tell us about it. Indeed, there is no prophet except that he has an angel who brings him the news. So tell us: who is your companion?" He said: "Gabriel." They said: "Gabriel is the one who descends with destruction, fighting, and punishment, our enemy. If you had said Michael, who descends with mercy, plants, and rain, it would have been [acceptable]." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel...﴾ (al-Baqarah: 97) to the end of the verse.

Al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *al-Matar*, and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that whenever he heard the sound of thunder, he would say: "Glory be to the One whom it glorifies," and he said: "Thunder is an angel who drives the rain-clouds as the shepherd drives his sheep."

Similar to this has been narrated from him through several chains.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah that thunder is the voice of an angel. Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated something similar from Ibn 'Umar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Thunder is an angel named Ar-Ra'd (Thunder), and this sound is its glorification. When its driving becomes intense, the clouds rub together and blaze from its fear, and the lightning bolts come out from between them."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Kharaʾiti, and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* narrated from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, who said: "Indeed there are seas of fire below the Throne, from which the lightning bolts come."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "The lightning bolts are fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and He is severe in might﴾, that he said: "Severe in strength."

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ali, who said: "Severe in seizing."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning His words ﴿To Him is the true call﴾, that he said: "The monotheism: there is no god but Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿the call of truth﴾, that he said: "The testimony that there is no god but Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ali concerning His words ﴿except like one who stretches out his hands toward water that it may reach his mouth, but it will not reach it﴾, that he said: "The thirsty man would stretch out his hand toward the well so that the water would rise to him, but it would not reach him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: "This is the example of the polytheist who worships another alongside Allah. His example is like the example of the thirsty man who looks at his reflection in the water from afar, wanting to reach it, but he is unable to."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning His words ﴿Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾, that he said: "The believer and the disbeliever."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him concerning His words ﴿He sent down water from the sky﴾, to the end of the verse, that he said: "This is an example which Allah has coined. Hearts take from it according to the degree of their certainty and doubt. As for doubt, no deed benefits with it. As for certainty, Allah benefits its people with it. This is His words: ﴿As for the foam, it passes away as scum﴾, which is doubt, ﴿but what benefits people remains on the earth﴾, which is certainty. And just as ornaments are placed in fire so that their pure part is taken and their dross is left, so Allah accepts certainty and leaves doubt."

These same narrators also narrated from him concerning ﴿The valleys flowed each according to its measure﴾, that he said: "The small [flows] according to its smallness, and the large according to its largeness."

When He, glory be to Him, frightened His servants with the sending down of what cannot be averted, He followed it with matters that in some respects give hope and in others cause fear: lightning, clouds, thunder, and thunderbolt. The meanings of these words and their causes were explained at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

There is disagreement about the grammatical status of ﴿khawfan wa-ṭamaʿan﴾ ("in fear and in hope"). It has been said that it is an absolute object (maṣdar, a verbal noun used as an accusative of cognate meaning), i.e., "so that you fear and so that you hope, a hope." It has been said that it is an accusative of purpose (ʿillah), on the assumption of the intention of fear and hope, so that the subject of the causative verb and the subject of the object of purpose do not differ. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring to the lightning, or to the addressees, with the sense "people who are fearful." Other views have been held that have no need to be mentioned.

It has been said: the fear is that which arises from the thunderbolts, and the hope is that which arises from the rain.

Al-Zajjāj said: the fear is for the traveller, because of what harms him from the rain, and the hope is for the resident, because when he sees the lightning he hopes for the rain, which is the cause of fertility.

﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾: the definite article here is generic (li-l-jins), and the singular is saḥābah (a cloud). "Thiqāl" is the plural of thaqīlah (heavy).

The meaning is that God, glory be to Him, makes the clouds that He produces heavy by the water He places in them.

﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾: that is, the thunder itself glorifies God with the praise of God, meaning in a state of being joined with His praise. This is not improbable, and there is nothing to prevent God from causing it to speak thus: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 44].

As for interpreting "the thunder" as an angel among the angels, there is no improbability in that either. Its mention in the singular, followed by the mention of the angels after it, would be for additional distinction and special care. It has been said that the meaning is: the hearers of the thunder glorify, that is, they say, "Glory be to God and praise be to God." ﴿And the angels, out of fear of Him﴾: that is, the angels glorify out of fear of God, glory be to Him. It has been said: out of fear of the thunder.

A group of exegetes have mentioned that these angels are the helpers of the thunder, and that God, glory be to Him, made for it helpers.

﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾ among His creatures, so that He destroys him. The context of these matters here serves the purpose for which the preceding verses were brought, which is the demonstration of the perfection of His power.

﴿Yet they dispute concerning God﴾: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers addressed in His saying "It is He who shows you the lightning." That is: these disbelievers, despite these signs which God showed them, dispute concerning the affair of God, glory be to Him. They deny the resurrection at one time, and at another they seek to hasten the punishment; they deny the messengers and disobey God. This clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it is permissible that it be a resumed (istiʾnāfiyyah) clause.

﴿And He is severe in might (miḥāl)﴾: Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: al-miḥāl is cunning, and cunning from God is planning with truth.

Al-Naḥḥās said: cunning from God is bringing harm upon the one who deserves it from a direction he does not perceive.

Al-Azharī said: al-miḥāl is strength and vehemence, and the letter mīm is original (not augmentative); one says māḥaltu fulānan miḥālan, "whichever of us is stronger."

Abū ʿUbayd said: al-miḥāl is punishment and harm.

Al-Zajjāj said: one says māḥaltuhu miḥālan when you contend with him until it becomes clear which of you is stronger, and al-maḥl in the language means vehemence.

Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, severe in guile. Its origin is from stratagem, and the mīm was made like the mīm of place (mafʿal); its origin is from being established (al-kawn), then one says tamakkantu.

Al-Azharī said: Ibn Qutaybah erred in claiming that the mīm in it is augmentative; rather it is original. Whenever you see a word in the pattern fiʿāl whose first letter is a kasrah-vowelled mīm, it is original, like mihād, milāk, and mirās, and other such words.

Al-Aʿraj read ﴿and He is severe in might﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm (maḥāl). This reading has been interpreted as meaning "power" (ḥawl).

Among the Companions and the Successors there are eight opinions on the interpretation of al-miḥāl here: the first is enmity; the second is power (ḥawl); the third is seizing; the fourth is rancour; the fifth is strength; the sixth is anger; the seventh is destruction; the eighth is stratagem.

﴿To Him is the call of truth (daʿwat al-ḥaqq)﴾: the attribution of the call to truth is an attribution of association: that is, the call that is associated with truth, specific to Him, into which falsehood has no entry in any way, just as one says "the word of truth." The meaning is that it is an answered call, fulfilled in its proper place, unlike the call of those other than Him.

It has been said: the truth is God, glory be to Him, and the meaning is that for God, glory be to Him, is the call of the One who is truly called, who hears and responds.

It has been said: the intended meaning of the call of truth here is the word of monotheism and sincerity, and the meaning is: for God, from among His creatures, is that they should affirm His oneness and be sincere to Him.

It has been said: the call of truth is calling upon Him, glory be to Him, at the time of fear, for no one else is called upon at that time, as He said: ﴿Those whom you call upon fall away, except Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 67].

It has been said: the call is worship, for the worship of God is the truth and the reality.

﴿And those who call upon others besides Him do not respond to them with anything﴾: that is, the gods whom the disbelievers call upon besides God, mighty and majestic, do not respond to them with anything of what they ask of them, whatever it may be, except a response like the response of water to one who spreads his palms toward it from afar. For it does not respond to him, because it is inanimate and does not perceive his need for it, nor does it know that he asked it to reach his mouth. Hence He said: ﴿nor is it (the water) reaching him﴾, that is, the water does not reach into him.

Al-Zajjāj said: it is like the response given to one who spreads his palms toward water, calling the water to his mouth, and the water does not respond. God, glory be to Him, informed them that their calling upon the idols is like the calling of a thirsty man upon water, asking it to reach his mouth, and the water does not reach it.

It has been said: the meaning is that he is like one who spreads his hands toward water in order to grasp it, but nothing of it attains his palm. The Arabs have struck the proverb of grasping water for one who strives after what he cannot attain, as the poet said:

"So I became, from what was between me and her of affection, like one who grasps water in his hand."

And another said:

"Whoever trusts in this world becomes like one who grasps water, whose hand is betrayed by the gaps between his fingers."

Al-Farrāʾ said: the water here is the water of a well, because the well is a source of water. He likened the one who extends his hand to the well without a rope to one who calls upon others among the idols. God, glory be to Him, struck this as a parable for one who calls upon other than Him.

﴿And the call of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾: that is, that call goes astray from them, so they find nothing from it, and it benefits them in no way at all; rather it is lost and gone.

﴿And to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾: If by prostration is meant its literal meaning, which is placing the forehead on the ground in glorification with humility and submission, then this is evident regarding the believers, the angels, and the Muslim jinn. As for the disbelievers, it is not valid to interpret prostration in this sense concerning them. Therefore prostration mentioned in the verse must be understood in the sense that prostration is due to God and is required, so that it includes prostration in deed and other than it; or prostration is interpreted as submission, for the disbelievers, although they do not prostrate to God, glory be to Him, are nonetheless subject to His command and judgement regarding them in health and sickness, life and death, poverty and wealth. What confirms this meaning is His saying: ﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾, for the disbelievers submit unwillingly as the believers submit willingly. Both are in the accusative as maṣdar (verbal noun): that is, submission of willingness and submission of unwillingness; or as circumstantial accusatives: willing and unwilling.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the verse is specific to the believers, for they prostrate willingly, while some disbelievers prostrate under compulsion and fear, like the hypocrites; so the verse is understood as referring to these. It has been said: the verse refers to the believers, among whom some prostrate willingly, for whom prostration is not burdensome, and some for whom it is burdensome, because accepting the obligation is a hardship; but they bear the hardship out of faith in God and sincerity to Him.

﴿And their shadows, in the mornings and the evenings﴾: "shadows" is the plural of shadow (ẓill), and what is meant by it is the shadow of a person that follows him. It is made to prostrate by his prostration, since it becomes inseparable from him and never leaves him.

Al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Anbārī said: it is not unlikely that God creates for the shadows understandings by which they prostrate to God, glory be to Him, just as He gave understanding to the mountains so that they were occupied with His glorification. Thus the shadow of the believer prostrates to God willingly, and the shadow of the disbeliever prostrates to God unwillingly.

The mornings and evenings are singled out for mention because the shadows become most apparent at these two times. They are the time-adverb for the implied prostration: that is, their shadows prostrate at these two times.

The interpretation of "mornings and evenings" has been mentioned in al-Aʿrāf. Among what has the same meaning as this verse is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Have they not seen that whatever thing God has created, its shadows incline from right and left, prostrating to God, and they are humbled?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 48].

He used "man" (who) in ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ by way of giving precedence to rational beings over others, and because the prostration of others is a consequence of their prostration. Among what supports understanding prostration as submission is that the placing of "to God" before the verb conveys exclusivity, for the prostration of the disbelievers to their idols is well known, and they do not submit to them in the way they submit to God in matters which they themselves acknowledge to be from God, such as creation, life, death, and the like.

﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?﴾ God, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger to ask the disbelievers: who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Then, since they were acknowledging this and confessing it, as God, glory be to Him, related in His saying: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: they were created by the Mighty, the Knowing﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9], and His saying ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say: God﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87], He commanded His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to answer, so He said: ﴿Say: God﴾. It is as if He related their answer and what they believe, because they might falter in answering out of fear of what would be binding on them. Then He commanded him to impose the proof upon them and confound them, so He said: ﴿Say: Have you then taken, besides Him, protectors?﴾ The interrogative is for denial: that is, if the Lord of the heavens and the earth is God, as you acknowledge and confess, as He related about you in His saying: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne? They will say: God﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 86–87].

Then how is it that you have taken for yourselves, besides Him, protectors who are powerless, ﴿who possess no benefit for themselves﴾, bringing benefit to themselves by it, ﴿nor harm﴾, causing harm to others by it or warding off harm from themselves? So how do you hope for benefit and harm from them when they do not possess either for themselves? The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

Then God, glory be to Him, struck a parable for them and commanded His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say it to them. So He said: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ That is: is the blind man in his religion, who is the disbeliever, equal to the seeing man in it, who is the monotheist? For the former is ignorant of what is obligatory for him and what is binding on him, while the latter knows that.

Ibn Muḥayṣin, Abū Bakr, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "Or are the darkness and the light equal?" with the yāʾ (third person), and the rest read it with the tāʾ (second person). Abū ʿUbayd preferred the second reading.

The darkness refers to disbelief, and the light to faith. The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach: that is, how can they be equal when between them there is the same disparity as between the blind and the seeing, and between darkness and light? The light is in the singular and the darkness in the plural, because the path of truth is one and does not differ, while the paths of falsehood are many and not limited.

﴿Or have they set up for God partners who created as He created, so that the creation seemed alike to them?﴾ The particle "am" here is the disjunctive one, which means "rather" together with the hamzah: that is, rather, have they made for God partners who created as He created? The interrogative is for denying that this has occurred.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: its meaning is: have they made for God partners who created the like of what God created, so that the creation of the partners became similar to the creation of God in their view? That is, the matter is not so, that the affair should be confused for them; rather, if they reflect with their minds, they will find that God is the one alone who creates, while the rest of the partners create nothing. The clause ﴿who created as He created﴾ is in the accusative position as a descriptive clause of "partners."

The meaning is: they did not set up partners for God who share in creating as He creates, so that "the creation" would be confused for them by this cause, and so deserve worship from them. Rather, they set up idols and the like as partners to Him, and those are far from being like that. Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to make the truth clear to them and guide them to what is right, so He said: ﴿Say: "God is the Creator of all things,"﴾ whatever they may be, and no one else has any share in that in any way whatsoever.

Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and Qur'an exegete) said: The meaning is that He is the Creator of everything that can be created. Do you not see that He, exalted is He, is a "thing" but is not created? ﴿And He is the One,﴾ that is, the Sole in lordship, the Subduer over everything besides Him. So everything other than Him is a subject, subdued and overcome.

Then God, glorified is He, struck another parable for the truth and its adherents, and for falsehood and its claimants. He said: ﴿He sends down water from the sky,﴾ that is, from its direction. The indefiniteness of "water" (māʾan) is for abundance or for kind. ﴿So valleys flow according to their measure﴾ (awdiyah, plural of wādī, which is any open space between two mountains or the like).

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi (a grammarian) said: We know of no active participle (fāʿil) pluralized on the pattern afʿilah except this one. It seems it was treated as if it were on the pattern faʿīl, and so pluralized as afʿilah, like jarīb and ajribah. Just as faʿīl was treated as fāʿil and so pluralized as afʿāl, like yatīm and aytām, sharīf and ashrāf, and as aṣḥāb and anṣār for ṣāḥib and nāṣir. He said: In His words ﴿so valleys flow﴾ there is a figurative expression (tawassuʿ), meaning: its water flowed. He said: The meaning of "according to their measure" is according to the measure of their water, because the valleys did not flow by their own measure.

Al-Wahidi said: The qadar (measure) is the extent of a thing. The meaning: according to their measure of water. If the valley is small, little water flows; if it is wide, much water flows. In al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) it says: "according to their measure" means according to the amount which God knows to be beneficial to those on whom it rains and not harmful. Ibn al-Anbari said: The descent of the Qur'an, which gathers guidance and clarity, is likened to the descent of rain, since the benefit of the Qur'an's descent is general, as the benefit of rain's descent is general. The valleys are likened to hearts, since water settles in valleys as the Qur'an and faith settle in the hearts of believers. ﴿So the torrent carried a swelling foam.﴾ Zabad (foam) is the white, raised, puffed-up thing on the surface of the torrent, also called ghuthāʾ (scum) and rughwah (froth). Rābī (swelling) is what is high and raised above the water.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is what floats on the water. Others said: It is what increases because of its swelling, from rabā yarbū, meaning it increased.

What is meant by this is the likening of disbelief to the foam that rises on water: it vanishes, clings to the edges of the valley, and the winds drive it away. Likewise, disbelief departs and vanishes.

The first parable is complete. Then God, glorified is He, began to mention the second parable, so He said: ﴿And from what they heat in the fire﴾ (min, for the beginning of the extent: from it arises foam like the foam of water; or partitive: some of it is foam like it). The pronoun refers to humankind, left implicit because it is clear from context. This is according to the reading "yūqidūna" with the yāʾ (third person), which Ḥumayd, Ibn Muḥaysin, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ recited. The rest read it with the tāʾ (second person, address), and Abu ʿUbayd preferred the first reading.

The meaning: ﴿and from what you heat in the fire,﴾ so that what is molten of the substances that melt, ﴿seeking an ornament,﴾ that is, seeking to make ornaments with which you adorn and beautify yourselves, like gold and silver, ﴿or a commodity,﴾ that is, or seeking a commodity you enjoy, from vessels and tools made of iron, brass, copper, and lead, ﴿there is foam like it.﴾ The foam here means the dross, for it rises above what is melted of those substances, just as foam rises on water. So the pronoun in "like it" refers to ﴿a swelling foam﴾, and "foam" (zabad) is the subject, its predicate being ﴿from what they heat﴾.

﴿Thus God strikes the parables of truth and falsehood.﴾ That is, in the likeness of that wondrous striking, God strikes the parable of truth and the parable of falsehood. Then He began to divide the parable, so He said: ﴿As for the foam, it passes away as scum (jufāʾ).﴾ One says: "jafaʾa al-wādī" (with hamza) jufāʾan, when the valley casts out filth and foam.

Al-Farraʾ said: al-jufāʾ is the casting out. One says: the valley cast out its scum (ghuthāʾahu) as jufāʾ, when it threw it away. Jufāʾ is in the position of ghuthāʾ.

Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said the same. Abu ʿUbaydah related that he heard Ruʾbah recite "jufālan."

Abu ʿUbaydah said: One says "ajfalat al-qidr" when the pot casts out its foam, and "ajfalat al-rīḥ al-saḥāb" when the wind cuts through the clouds.

Abu Ḥātim said: Ruʾbah's reading is not to be recited, because he used to eat mice.

Know that the aspect of likeness between the two foams, in the foam that the torrent carries and the foam that rises on the heated substances, is that when the earth's dust mixed with the water and carried it along, it became a swelling foam above it. Likewise, what is heated in the fire until the melting substances melt: their origin is from the minerals that grow in the earth, and dust mixes with them. When they are melted, that dust which mixed with them becomes dross raised above them.

﴿As for what benefits people,﴾ from these two, which is the pure water and the pure molten substance free of dross, ﴿it remains in the earth,﴾ that is, it stays there. As for the water, it runs through the veins of the earth, and people benefit from it. As for what is melted of those substances, it is fashioned into ornaments and goods. These are two parables God struck for truth and falsehood. He says: falsehood, even if it appears over truth at times and rises above it, God, glorified is He, will surely erase it and annul it, and make the final outcome belong to the truth and its people. It is like the foam that rises on water, which the water casts away and which vanishes, and like the dross of those substances, which, though it rises over them, the furnace casts out and expels. This is the parable of falsehood. As for the water that benefits people and makes pastures grow, it remains in the earth. Likewise, the pure part of those substances remains pure, with no admixture. This is the parable of truth.

Al-Zajjaj said: The parable of the believer, his belief, and the benefit of faith is like the parable of this water which is used for the growth of the earth and the life of everything. It is also like the benefit of silver, gold, and all precious substances, for all of these remain as useful things. The parable of the disbeliever and his disbelief is like the foam which passes away as scum, and like the dross of iron and what the fire expels from the filth of silver and gold, which is of no use.

We have already related from Ibn al-Anbari, above, that he likened the descent of the Qur'an, and so on to the end of what we mentioned, and made that a parable God struck for the Qur'an. ﴿Thus God strikes parables,﴾ that is, in the likeness of that wondrous striking, God strikes parables in every matter, out of complete care for His servants and gentleness toward them. This is an emphasis on His words: ﴿Thus God strikes the truth and falsehood.﴾

Then God, glorified is He, explained who among His servants were the subjects of the parable of truth and the parable of falsehood. Regarding those for whom the parable of truth was struck, He said: ﴿For those who answered their Lord﴾ (that is, who responded to His call when He summoned them to His oneness, to affirm His messengers, and to act by His laws), ﴿is the best (al-ḥusnā)﴾, an adjective for an omitted noun: that is, the best reward, which is Paradise. Regarding those for whom the parable of falsehood was struck, He said: ﴿And those who did not answer Him﴾ (that is, His call to what He summoned them to), the relative clause is the subject, and its predicate is the conditional sentence: ﴿if they had all that is in the earth together﴾ of kinds of wealth which servants possess and gather, such that none of it would leave their ownership, ﴿and the like of it with it,﴾ that is, the like of all that is in the earth, existing alongside it and added to it, ﴿they would ransom themselves with it.﴾ That is, with all that was mentioned, which is what is in the earth and its like.

The meaning: to free themselves by it from the great punishment and the terrible horror they are in. Then God, glorified is He, explained what He had prepared for them, saying: ﴿Those, for them is the evil reckoning.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: Because their disbelief nullified their deeds. Others said: the evil reckoning is the strict scrutiny of it; and it was said: it is that a man is called to account for all his sin, and none of it is forgiven. ﴿Their abode is Hell,﴾ that is, their return is to it. ﴿And how wretched is the resting place,﴾ that is, the place where they settle.

The one singled out for blame is omitted.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as fear and hope﴾: He said: fear for the traveler, who fears its harm and hardship; and hope for the resident, who hopes for God's provision and hopes for the blessing and benefit of rain.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan who said: fear for the people of the sea, and hope for the people of the land.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak who said: the fear is what is feared from thunderbolts, and the hope is the rain.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Kharaʾiti in Makarim al-Akhlaq, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related through several chains from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib who said: Lightning is torches of fire in the hands of the angels of the clouds, with which they drive the clouds.

It is related from a group of the early generation what agrees with this and what contradicts it, and perhaps we have already mentioned some of that in Surat al-Baqarah.

Ahmad related from a shaykh of the Banu Ghifar who had accompanied the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "God creates the clouds, and they speak in the best speech, and laugh in the best laugh." It was said: the intended meaning of their speech is thunder, and of their laughter is lightning.

It is established with Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi in al-Yawm wa al-Layla, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard thunder and thunderbolts, he said: 'O God, do not kill us with Your wrath, do not destroy us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that.'"

Al-ʿUqayli related it and declared it weak, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God creates the clouds, then sends down water in them. There is nothing more beautiful than their laughter, nor more beautiful than their speech. Their speech is thunder and their laughter is lightning."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that Khuzaymah ibn Thabit, not the Ansari, "asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the origin of the clouds. He said: 'An angel assigned to them gathers the distant and joins the near, with a torch in his hand. When he raises it, it flashes; when he drives, it thunders; and when he strikes, it bursts (into thunderbolts).'"

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasaʾi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dalaʾil, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, we will ask you about five things. If you inform us of them, we will know you are a prophet and follow you.' He took from them the covenant that Israel took from his sons when he said: ﴿God is Witness over what we say.﴾ He said: 'Ask.' They said: 'Tell us about the sign of the prophet.' He said: 'His eyes sleep but his heart does not sleep.' They said: 'Tell us how a woman produces a female child and how a male child.' He said: 'The two waters meet; if the man's water rises above the woman's, a male is produced, and if the woman's water rises above the man's, a female is produced.' They said: 'Tell us what Israel forbade to himself.' He said: 'He suffered from sciatica, and found nothing that suited him except the milk of such-and-such,' meaning camels, 'so he forbade their meat.' They said: 'You have spoken truly.' They said: 'Tell us what this thunder is.' He said: 'An angel of God's angels assigned to the clouds, with a torch of fire in his hand, with which he drives the clouds wherever God commands him.' They said: 'Then what is this voice that we hear?' He said: 'Its voice.'"

They said: "You have spoken the truth. Only one remains, and it is the one we will follow you in if you tell us about it. Indeed, there is no prophet except that he has an angel who brings him the news. So tell us: who is your companion?" He said: "Gabriel." They said: "Gabriel is the one who descends with destruction, fighting, and punishment, our enemy. If you had said Michael, who descends with mercy, plants, and rain, it would have been [acceptable]." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel...﴾ (al-Baqarah: 97) to the end of the verse.

Al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *al-Matar*, and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that whenever he heard the sound of thunder, he would say: "Glory be to the One whom it glorifies," and he said: "Thunder is an angel who drives the rain-clouds as the shepherd drives his sheep."

Similar to this has been narrated from him through several chains.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah that thunder is the voice of an angel. Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated something similar from Ibn 'Umar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Thunder is an angel named Ar-Ra'd (Thunder), and this sound is its glorification. When its driving becomes intense, the clouds rub together and blaze from its fear, and the lightning bolts come out from between them."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Kharaʾiti, and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* narrated from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, who said: "Indeed there are seas of fire below the Throne, from which the lightning bolts come."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "The lightning bolts are fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and He is severe in might﴾, that he said: "Severe in strength."

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ali, who said: "Severe in seizing."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning His words ﴿To Him is the true call﴾, that he said: "The monotheism: there is no god but Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿the call of truth﴾, that he said: "The testimony that there is no god but Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ali concerning His words ﴿except like one who stretches out his hands toward water that it may reach his mouth, but it will not reach it﴾, that he said: "The thirsty man would stretch out his hand toward the well so that the water would rise to him, but it would not reach him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: "This is the example of the polytheist who worships another alongside Allah. His example is like the example of the thirsty man who looks at his reflection in the water from afar, wanting to reach it, but he is unable to."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning His words ﴿Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾, that he said: "The believer and the disbeliever."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him concerning His words ﴿He sent down water from the sky﴾, to the end of the verse, that he said: "This is an example which Allah has coined. Hearts take from it according to the degree of their certainty and doubt. As for doubt, no deed benefits with it. As for certainty, Allah benefits its people with it. This is His words: ﴿As for the foam, it passes away as scum﴾, which is doubt, ﴿but what benefits people remains on the earth﴾, which is certainty. And just as ornaments are placed in fire so that their pure part is taken and their dross is left, so Allah accepts certainty and leaves doubt."

These same narrators also narrated from him concerning ﴿The valleys flowed each according to its measure﴾, that he said: "The small [flows] according to its smallness, and the large according to its largeness."

When He, glory be to Him, frightened His servants with the sending down of what cannot be averted, He followed it with matters that in some respects give hope and in others cause fear: lightning, clouds, thunder, and thunderbolt. The meanings of these words and their causes were explained at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

There is disagreement about the grammatical status of ﴿khawfan wa-ṭamaʿan﴾ ("in fear and in hope"). It has been said that it is an absolute object (maṣdar, a verbal noun used as an accusative of cognate meaning), i.e., "so that you fear and so that you hope, a hope." It has been said that it is an accusative of purpose (ʿillah), on the assumption of the intention of fear and hope, so that the subject of the causative verb and the subject of the object of purpose do not differ. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring to the lightning, or to the addressees, with the sense "people who are fearful." Other views have been held that have no need to be mentioned.

It has been said: the fear is that which arises from the thunderbolts, and the hope is that which arises from the rain.

Al-Zajjāj said: the fear is for the traveller, because of what harms him from the rain, and the hope is for the resident, because when he sees the lightning he hopes for the rain, which is the cause of fertility.

﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾: the definite article here is generic (li-l-jins), and the singular is saḥābah (a cloud). "Thiqāl" is the plural of thaqīlah (heavy).

The meaning is that God, glory be to Him, makes the clouds that He produces heavy by the water He places in them.

﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾: that is, the thunder itself glorifies God with the praise of God, meaning in a state of being joined with His praise. This is not improbable, and there is nothing to prevent God from causing it to speak thus: ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 44].

As for interpreting "the thunder" as an angel among the angels, there is no improbability in that either. Its mention in the singular, followed by the mention of the angels after it, would be for additional distinction and special care. It has been said that the meaning is: the hearers of the thunder glorify, that is, they say, "Glory be to God and praise be to God." ﴿And the angels, out of fear of Him﴾: that is, the angels glorify out of fear of God, glory be to Him. It has been said: out of fear of the thunder.

A group of exegetes have mentioned that these angels are the helpers of the thunder, and that God, glory be to Him, made for it helpers.

﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾ among His creatures, so that He destroys him. The context of these matters here serves the purpose for which the preceding verses were brought, which is the demonstration of the perfection of His power.

﴿Yet they dispute concerning God﴾: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers addressed in His saying "It is He who shows you the lightning." That is: these disbelievers, despite these signs which God showed them, dispute concerning the affair of God, glory be to Him. They deny the resurrection at one time, and at another they seek to hasten the punishment; they deny the messengers and disobey God. This clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it is permissible that it be a resumed (istiʾnāfiyyah) clause.

﴿And He is severe in might (miḥāl)﴾: Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: al-miḥāl is cunning, and cunning from God is planning with truth.

Al-Naḥḥās said: cunning from God is bringing harm upon the one who deserves it from a direction he does not perceive.

Al-Azharī said: al-miḥāl is strength and vehemence, and the letter mīm is original (not augmentative); one says māḥaltu fulānan miḥālan, "whichever of us is stronger."

Abū ʿUbayd said: al-miḥāl is punishment and harm.

Al-Zajjāj said: one says māḥaltuhu miḥālan when you contend with him until it becomes clear which of you is stronger, and al-maḥl in the language means vehemence.

Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, severe in guile. Its origin is from stratagem, and the mīm was made like the mīm of place (mafʿal); its origin is from being established (al-kawn), then one says tamakkantu.

Al-Azharī said: Ibn Qutaybah erred in claiming that the mīm in it is augmentative; rather it is original. Whenever you see a word in the pattern fiʿāl whose first letter is a kasrah-vowelled mīm, it is original, like mihād, milāk, and mirās, and other such words.

Al-Aʿraj read ﴿and He is severe in might﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm (maḥāl). This reading has been interpreted as meaning "power" (ḥawl).

Among the Companions and the Successors there are eight opinions on the interpretation of al-miḥāl here: the first is enmity; the second is power (ḥawl); the third is seizing; the fourth is rancour; the fifth is strength; the sixth is anger; the seventh is destruction; the eighth is stratagem.

﴿To Him is the call of truth (daʿwat al-ḥaqq)﴾: the attribution of the call to truth is an attribution of association: that is, the call that is associated with truth, specific to Him, into which falsehood has no entry in any way, just as one says "the word of truth." The meaning is that it is an answered call, fulfilled in its proper place, unlike the call of those other than Him.

It has been said: the truth is God, glory be to Him, and the meaning is that for God, glory be to Him, is the call of the One who is truly called, who hears and responds.

It has been said: the intended meaning of the call of truth here is the word of monotheism and sincerity, and the meaning is: for God, from among His creatures, is that they should affirm His oneness and be sincere to Him.

It has been said: the call of truth is calling upon Him, glory be to Him, at the time of fear, for no one else is called upon at that time, as He said: ﴿Those whom you call upon fall away, except Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 67].

It has been said: the call is worship, for the worship of God is the truth and the reality.

﴿And those who call upon others besides Him do not respond to them with anything﴾: that is, the gods whom the disbelievers call upon besides God, mighty and majestic, do not respond to them with anything of what they ask of them, whatever it may be, except a response like the response of water to one who spreads his palms toward it from afar. For it does not respond to him, because it is inanimate and does not perceive his need for it, nor does it know that he asked it to reach his mouth. Hence He said: ﴿nor is it (the water) reaching him﴾, that is, the water does not reach into him.

Al-Zajjāj said: it is like the response given to one who spreads his palms toward water, calling the water to his mouth, and the water does not respond. God, glory be to Him, informed them that their calling upon the idols is like the calling of a thirsty man upon water, asking it to reach his mouth, and the water does not reach it.

It has been said: the meaning is that he is like one who spreads his hands toward water in order to grasp it, but nothing of it attains his palm. The Arabs have struck the proverb of grasping water for one who strives after what he cannot attain, as the poet said:

"So I became, from what was between me and her of affection, like one who grasps water in his hand."

And another said:

"Whoever trusts in this world becomes like one who grasps water, whose hand is betrayed by the gaps between his fingers."

Al-Farrāʾ said: the water here is the water of a well, because the well is a source of water. He likened the one who extends his hand to the well without a rope to one who calls upon others among the idols. God, glory be to Him, struck this as a parable for one who calls upon other than Him.

﴿And the call of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾: that is, that call goes astray from them, so they find nothing from it, and it benefits them in no way at all; rather it is lost and gone.

﴿And to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾: If by prostration is meant its literal meaning, which is placing the forehead on the ground in glorification with humility and submission, then this is evident regarding the believers, the angels, and the Muslim jinn. As for the disbelievers, it is not valid to interpret prostration in this sense concerning them. Therefore prostration mentioned in the verse must be understood in the sense that prostration is due to God and is required, so that it includes prostration in deed and other than it; or prostration is interpreted as submission, for the disbelievers, although they do not prostrate to God, glory be to Him, are nonetheless subject to His command and judgement regarding them in health and sickness, life and death, poverty and wealth. What confirms this meaning is His saying: ﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾, for the disbelievers submit unwillingly as the believers submit willingly. Both are in the accusative as maṣdar (verbal noun): that is, submission of willingness and submission of unwillingness; or as circumstantial accusatives: willing and unwilling.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the verse is specific to the believers, for they prostrate willingly, while some disbelievers prostrate under compulsion and fear, like the hypocrites; so the verse is understood as referring to these. It has been said: the verse refers to the believers, among whom some prostrate willingly, for whom prostration is not burdensome, and some for whom it is burdensome, because accepting the obligation is a hardship; but they bear the hardship out of faith in God and sincerity to Him.

﴿And their shadows, in the mornings and the evenings﴾: "shadows" is the plural of shadow (ẓill), and what is meant by it is the shadow of a person that follows him. It is made to prostrate by his prostration, since it becomes inseparable from him and never leaves him.

Al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Anbārī said: it is not unlikely that God creates for the shadows understandings by which they prostrate to God, glory be to Him, just as He gave understanding to the mountains so that they were occupied with His glorification. Thus the shadow of the believer prostrates to God willingly, and the shadow of the disbeliever prostrates to God unwillingly.

The mornings and evenings are singled out for mention because the shadows become most apparent at these two times. They are the time-adverb for the implied prostration: that is, their shadows prostrate at these two times.

The interpretation of "mornings and evenings" has been mentioned in al-Aʿrāf. Among what has the same meaning as this verse is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Have they not seen that whatever thing God has created, its shadows incline from right and left, prostrating to God, and they are humbled?﴾ [al-Naḥl: 48].

He used "man" (who) in ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ by way of giving precedence to rational beings over others, and because the prostration of others is a consequence of their prostration. Among what supports understanding prostration as submission is that the placing of "to God" before the verb conveys exclusivity, for the prostration of the disbelievers to their idols is well known, and they do not submit to them in the way they submit to God in matters which they themselves acknowledge to be from God, such as creation, life, death, and the like.

﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?﴾ God, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger to ask the disbelievers: who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Then, since they were acknowledging this and confessing it, as God, glory be to Him, related in His saying: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: they were created by the Mighty, the Knowing﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9], and His saying ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say: God﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87], He commanded His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to answer, so He said: ﴿Say: God﴾. It is as if He related their answer and what they believe, because they might falter in answering out of fear of what would be binding on them. Then He commanded him to impose the proof upon them and confound them, so He said: ﴿Say: Have you then taken, besides Him, protectors?﴾ The interrogative is for denial: that is, if the Lord of the heavens and the earth is God, as you acknowledge and confess, as He related about you in His saying: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne? They will say: God﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 86–87].

Then how is it that you have taken for yourselves, besides Him, protectors who are powerless, ﴿who possess no benefit for themselves﴾, bringing benefit to themselves by it, ﴿nor harm﴾, causing harm to others by it or warding off harm from themselves? So how do you hope for benefit and harm from them when they do not possess either for themselves? The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

Then God, glory be to Him, struck a parable for them and commanded His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say it to them. So He said: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ That is: is the blind man in his religion, who is the disbeliever, equal to the seeing man in it, who is the monotheist? For the former is ignorant of what is obligatory for him and what is binding on him, while the latter knows that.

Ibn Muḥayṣin, Abū Bakr, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "Or are the darkness and the light equal?" with the yāʾ (third person), and the rest read it with the tāʾ (second person). Abū ʿUbayd preferred the second reading.

The darkness refers to disbelief, and the light to faith. The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach: that is, how can they be equal when between them there is the same disparity as between the blind and the seeing, and between darkness and light? The light is in the singular and the darkness in the plural, because the path of truth is one and does not differ, while the paths of falsehood are many and not limited.

﴿Or have they set up for God partners who created as He created, so that the creation seemed alike to them?﴾ The particle "am" here is the disjunctive one, which means "rather" together with the hamzah: that is, rather, have they made for God partners who created as He created? The interrogative is for denying that this has occurred.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: its meaning is: have they made for God partners who created the like of what God created, so that the creation of the partners became similar to the creation of God in their view? That is, the matter is not so, that the affair should be confused for them; rather, if they reflect with their minds, they will find that God is the one alone who creates, while the rest of the partners create nothing. The clause ﴿who created as He created﴾ is in the accusative position as a descriptive clause of "partners."

The meaning is: they did not set up partners for God who share in creating as He creates, so that "the creation" would be confused for them by this cause, and so deserve worship from them. Rather, they set up idols and the like as partners to Him, and those are far from being like that. Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to make the truth clear to them and guide them to what is right, so He said: ﴿Say: "God is the Creator of all things,"﴾ whatever they may be, and no one else has any share in that in any way whatsoever.

Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and Qur'an exegete) said: The meaning is that He is the Creator of everything that can be created. Do you not see that He, exalted is He, is a "thing" but is not created? ﴿And He is the One,﴾ that is, the Sole in lordship, the Subduer over everything besides Him. So everything other than Him is a subject, subdued and overcome.

Then God, glorified is He, struck another parable for the truth and its adherents, and for falsehood and its claimants. He said: ﴿He sends down water from the sky,﴾ that is, from its direction. The indefiniteness of "water" (māʾan) is for abundance or for kind. ﴿So valleys flow according to their measure﴾ (awdiyah, plural of wādī, which is any open space between two mountains or the like).

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi (a grammarian) said: We know of no active participle (fāʿil) pluralized on the pattern afʿilah except this one. It seems it was treated as if it were on the pattern faʿīl, and so pluralized as afʿilah, like jarīb and ajribah. Just as faʿīl was treated as fāʿil and so pluralized as afʿāl, like yatīm and aytām, sharīf and ashrāf, and as aṣḥāb and anṣār for ṣāḥib and nāṣir. He said: In His words ﴿so valleys flow﴾ there is a figurative expression (tawassuʿ), meaning: its water flowed. He said: The meaning of "according to their measure" is according to the measure of their water, because the valleys did not flow by their own measure.

Al-Wahidi said: The qadar (measure) is the extent of a thing. The meaning: according to their measure of water. If the valley is small, little water flows; if it is wide, much water flows. In al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) it says: "according to their measure" means according to the amount which God knows to be beneficial to those on whom it rains and not harmful. Ibn al-Anbari said: The descent of the Qur'an, which gathers guidance and clarity, is likened to the descent of rain, since the benefit of the Qur'an's descent is general, as the benefit of rain's descent is general. The valleys are likened to hearts, since water settles in valleys as the Qur'an and faith settle in the hearts of believers. ﴿So the torrent carried a swelling foam.﴾ Zabad (foam) is the white, raised, puffed-up thing on the surface of the torrent, also called ghuthāʾ (scum) and rughwah (froth). Rābī (swelling) is what is high and raised above the water.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is what floats on the water. Others said: It is what increases because of its swelling, from rabā yarbū, meaning it increased.

What is meant by this is the likening of disbelief to the foam that rises on water: it vanishes, clings to the edges of the valley, and the winds drive it away. Likewise, disbelief departs and vanishes.

The first parable is complete. Then God, glorified is He, began to mention the second parable, so He said: ﴿And from what they heat in the fire﴾ (min, for the beginning of the extent: from it arises foam like the foam of water; or partitive: some of it is foam like it). The pronoun refers to humankind, left implicit because it is clear from context. This is according to the reading "yūqidūna" with the yāʾ (third person), which Ḥumayd, Ibn Muḥaysin, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ recited. The rest read it with the tāʾ (second person, address), and Abu ʿUbayd preferred the first reading.

The meaning: ﴿and from what you heat in the fire,﴾ so that what is molten of the substances that melt, ﴿seeking an ornament,﴾ that is, seeking to make ornaments with which you adorn and beautify yourselves, like gold and silver, ﴿or a commodity,﴾ that is, or seeking a commodity you enjoy, from vessels and tools made of iron, brass, copper, and lead, ﴿there is foam like it.﴾ The foam here means the dross, for it rises above what is melted of those substances, just as foam rises on water. So the pronoun in "like it" refers to ﴿a swelling foam﴾, and "foam" (zabad) is the subject, its predicate being ﴿from what they heat﴾.

﴿Thus God strikes the parables of truth and falsehood.﴾ That is, in the likeness of that wondrous striking, God strikes the parable of truth and the parable of falsehood. Then He began to divide the parable, so He said: ﴿As for the foam, it passes away as scum (jufāʾ).﴾ One says: "jafaʾa al-wādī" (with hamza) jufāʾan, when the valley casts out filth and foam.

Al-Farraʾ said: al-jufāʾ is the casting out. One says: the valley cast out its scum (ghuthāʾahu) as jufāʾ, when it threw it away. Jufāʾ is in the position of ghuthāʾ.

Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said the same. Abu ʿUbaydah related that he heard Ruʾbah recite "jufālan."

Abu ʿUbaydah said: One says "ajfalat al-qidr" when the pot casts out its foam, and "ajfalat al-rīḥ al-saḥāb" when the wind cuts through the clouds.

Abu Ḥātim said: Ruʾbah's reading is not to be recited, because he used to eat mice.

Know that the aspect of likeness between the two foams, in the foam that the torrent carries and the foam that rises on the heated substances, is that when the earth's dust mixed with the water and carried it along, it became a swelling foam above it. Likewise, what is heated in the fire until the melting substances melt: their origin is from the minerals that grow in the earth, and dust mixes with them. When they are melted, that dust which mixed with them becomes dross raised above them.

﴿As for what benefits people,﴾ from these two, which is the pure water and the pure molten substance free of dross, ﴿it remains in the earth,﴾ that is, it stays there. As for the water, it runs through the veins of the earth, and people benefit from it. As for what is melted of those substances, it is fashioned into ornaments and goods. These are two parables God struck for truth and falsehood. He says: falsehood, even if it appears over truth at times and rises above it, God, glorified is He, will surely erase it and annul it, and make the final outcome belong to the truth and its people. It is like the foam that rises on water, which the water casts away and which vanishes, and like the dross of those substances, which, though it rises over them, the furnace casts out and expels. This is the parable of falsehood. As for the water that benefits people and makes pastures grow, it remains in the earth. Likewise, the pure part of those substances remains pure, with no admixture. This is the parable of truth.

Al-Zajjaj said: The parable of the believer, his belief, and the benefit of faith is like the parable of this water which is used for the growth of the earth and the life of everything. It is also like the benefit of silver, gold, and all precious substances, for all of these remain as useful things. The parable of the disbeliever and his disbelief is like the foam which passes away as scum, and like the dross of iron and what the fire expels from the filth of silver and gold, which is of no use.

We have already related from Ibn al-Anbari, above, that he likened the descent of the Qur'an, and so on to the end of what we mentioned, and made that a parable God struck for the Qur'an. ﴿Thus God strikes parables,﴾ that is, in the likeness of that wondrous striking, God strikes parables in every matter, out of complete care for His servants and gentleness toward them. This is an emphasis on His words: ﴿Thus God strikes the truth and falsehood.﴾

Then God, glorified is He, explained who among His servants were the subjects of the parable of truth and the parable of falsehood. Regarding those for whom the parable of truth was struck, He said: ﴿For those who answered their Lord﴾ (that is, who responded to His call when He summoned them to His oneness, to affirm His messengers, and to act by His laws), ﴿is the best (al-ḥusnā)﴾, an adjective for an omitted noun: that is, the best reward, which is Paradise. Regarding those for whom the parable of falsehood was struck, He said: ﴿And those who did not answer Him﴾ (that is, His call to what He summoned them to), the relative clause is the subject, and its predicate is the conditional sentence: ﴿if they had all that is in the earth together﴾ of kinds of wealth which servants possess and gather, such that none of it would leave their ownership, ﴿and the like of it with it,﴾ that is, the like of all that is in the earth, existing alongside it and added to it, ﴿they would ransom themselves with it.﴾ That is, with all that was mentioned, which is what is in the earth and its like.

The meaning: to free themselves by it from the great punishment and the terrible horror they are in. Then God, glorified is He, explained what He had prepared for them, saying: ﴿Those, for them is the evil reckoning.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: Because their disbelief nullified their deeds. Others said: the evil reckoning is the strict scrutiny of it; and it was said: it is that a man is called to account for all his sin, and none of it is forgiven. ﴿Their abode is Hell,﴾ that is, their return is to it. ﴿And how wretched is the resting place,﴾ that is, the place where they settle.

The one singled out for blame is omitted.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as fear and hope﴾: He said: fear for the traveler, who fears its harm and hardship; and hope for the resident, who hopes for God's provision and hopes for the blessing and benefit of rain.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan who said: fear for the people of the sea, and hope for the people of the land.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak who said: the fear is what is feared from thunderbolts, and the hope is the rain.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Kharaʾiti in Makarim al-Akhlaq, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related through several chains from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib who said: Lightning is torches of fire in the hands of the angels of the clouds, with which they drive the clouds.

It is related from a group of the early generation what agrees with this and what contradicts it, and perhaps we have already mentioned some of that in Surat al-Baqarah.

Ahmad related from a shaykh of the Banu Ghifar who had accompanied the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "God creates the clouds, and they speak in the best speech, and laugh in the best laugh." It was said: the intended meaning of their speech is thunder, and of their laughter is lightning.

It is established with Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi in al-Yawm wa al-Layla, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard thunder and thunderbolts, he said: 'O God, do not kill us with Your wrath, do not destroy us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that.'"

Al-ʿUqayli related it and declared it weak, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God creates the clouds, then sends down water in them. There is nothing more beautiful than their laughter, nor more beautiful than their speech. Their speech is thunder and their laughter is lightning."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah that Khuzaymah ibn Thabit, not the Ansari, "asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the origin of the clouds. He said: 'An angel assigned to them gathers the distant and joins the near, with a torch in his hand. When he raises it, it flashes; when he drives, it thunders; and when he strikes, it bursts (into thunderbolts).'"

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasaʾi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dalaʾil, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, we will ask you about five things. If you inform us of them, we will know you are a prophet and follow you.' He took from them the covenant that Israel took from his sons when he said: ﴿God is Witness over what we say.﴾ He said: 'Ask.' They said: 'Tell us about the sign of the prophet.' He said: 'His eyes sleep but his heart does not sleep.' They said: 'Tell us how a woman produces a female child and how a male child.' He said: 'The two waters meet; if the man's water rises above the woman's, a male is produced, and if the woman's water rises above the man's, a female is produced.' They said: 'Tell us what Israel forbade to himself.' He said: 'He suffered from sciatica, and found nothing that suited him except the milk of such-and-such,' meaning camels, 'so he forbade their meat.' They said: 'You have spoken truly.' They said: 'Tell us what this thunder is.' He said: 'An angel of God's angels assigned to the clouds, with a torch of fire in his hand, with which he drives the clouds wherever God commands him.' They said: 'Then what is this voice that we hear?' He said: 'Its voice.'"

They said: "You have spoken the truth. Only one remains, and it is the one we will follow you in if you tell us about it. Indeed, there is no prophet except that he has an angel who brings him the news. So tell us: who is your companion?" He said: "Gabriel." They said: "Gabriel is the one who descends with destruction, fighting, and punishment, our enemy. If you had said Michael, who descends with mercy, plants, and rain, it would have been [acceptable]." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel...﴾ (al-Baqarah: 97) to the end of the verse.

Al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *al-Matar*, and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that whenever he heard the sound of thunder, he would say: "Glory be to the One whom it glorifies," and he said: "Thunder is an angel who drives the rain-clouds as the shepherd drives his sheep."

Similar to this has been narrated from him through several chains.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah that thunder is the voice of an angel. Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated something similar from Ibn 'Umar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Thunder is an angel named Ar-Ra'd (Thunder), and this sound is its glorification. When its driving becomes intense, the clouds rub together and blaze from its fear, and the lightning bolts come out from between them."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Kharaʾiti, and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* narrated from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, who said: "Indeed there are seas of fire below the Throne, from which the lightning bolts come."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "The lightning bolts are fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and He is severe in might﴾, that he said: "Severe in strength."

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ali, who said: "Severe in seizing."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning His words ﴿To Him is the true call﴾, that he said: "The monotheism: there is no god but Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿the call of truth﴾, that he said: "The testimony that there is no god but Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ali concerning His words ﴿except like one who stretches out his hands toward water that it may reach his mouth, but it will not reach it﴾, that he said: "The thirsty man would stretch out his hand toward the well so that the water would rise to him, but it would not reach him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: "This is the example of the polytheist who worships another alongside Allah. His example is like the example of the thirsty man who looks at his reflection in the water from afar, wanting to reach it, but he is unable to."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning His words ﴿Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾, that he said: "The believer and the disbeliever."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him concerning His words ﴿He sent down water from the sky﴾, to the end of the verse, that he said: "This is an example which Allah has coined. Hearts take from it according to the degree of their certainty and doubt. As for doubt, no deed benefits with it. As for certainty, Allah benefits its people with it. This is His words: ﴿As for the foam, it passes away as scum﴾, which is doubt, ﴿but what benefits people remains on the earth﴾, which is certainty. And just as ornaments are placed in fire so that their pure part is taken and their dross is left, so Allah accepts certainty and leaves doubt."

These same narrators also narrated from him concerning ﴿The valleys flowed each according to its measure﴾, that he said: "The small [flows] according to its smallness, and the large according to its largeness."

When He, glory be to Him, frightened His servants with the sending down of what cannot be averted, He followed it with matters that in some respects give hope and in others cause fear: lightning, clouds, thunder, and thunderbolt. The meanings of these words and their causes were explained at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

There is disagreement about the grammatical status of ﴿khawfan wa-ṭamaʿan﴾ ("in fear and in hope"). It has been said that it is an absolute object (maṣdar, a verbal noun used as an accusative of cognate meaning), i.e., "so that you fear and so that you hope, a hope." It has been said that it is an accusative of purpose (ʿillah), on the assumption of the intention of fear and hope, so that the subject of the causative verb and the subject of the object of purpose do not differ.
