Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 13, verses 26–30:

When God, glorified is He, mentioned the end of the polytheists with His words, "And theirs will be the evil abode," someone might say: "We see many of them whom God has granted abundant provision and expanded it for them." He answered this with His words: ﴿God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it.﴾ So He may extend provision to one who is a disbeliever, and restrict it for one who is a believer, as a trial and a test. Expansion is not a sign of honour, nor restriction a sign of humiliation. The meaning of "yaqdir" (restricts) is: He constricts.

From this is His saying: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], meaning: constricted. It was also said: the meaning of "yaqdir" is: He gives according to what suffices. The meaning of the verse is that He alone is the doer of that, and He alone has power over it, not any other.

﴿And they rejoice in the worldly life﴾, meaning the polytheists of Makkah rejoiced in the world and were ignorant of what is with God. It has been said: in this verse there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir).

The estimated sense is: "Those who break the covenant of God after its binding, and sever what God has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth, and rejoice in the worldly life." Then "and they rejoice" is conjoined to "cause corruption."

﴿And the worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is but a enjoyment﴾, meaning it is only a thing to be enjoyed. It was also said: "matā'" is the singular of "amti'ah" (goods/utensils), like a bowl or a cup and the like. It was also said: the meaning is: a small thing that passes away, from "matā'a al-nahār" when the day rises, so it must end. It was also said: it is provision like the provision of a traveller, by which one takes provisions from it to the Hereafter.

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?"﴾ meaning: those polytheists of Makkah say, "Why was a sign not sent down upon Muhammad from his Lord?" The explanation of this has been given shortly before and repeated in several places.

﴿Say: "Indeed God misguides whom He wills"﴾: God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them with this, namely that misguidance is by the will of God, glorified is He; whoever He wills to misguide, goes astray, just as those who said, "Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?" went astray.

﴿And guides to Him whoever turns back [in repentance]﴾, meaning: and guides to the truth; or to Islam; or to His presence, mighty and majestic, whoever turns back, i.e., whoever returns to God in repentance and desists from what he was upon. The original meaning of "inābah" is entering into the course of good. So said al-Nisaburi.

The position of "those who believe" is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "whoever turns back," meaning they are those whom God guided and who turned to Him. It is also permissible that "those who believe" be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are those who believe," or that it be in the accusative by way of praise.

﴿And their hearts find rest in the remembrance of God﴾, meaning they become calm and find comfort in the remembrance of God, glorified is He, by their tongues, such as the recitation of the Qur'an, tasbih (saying "Subhan Allah"), tahmid (saying "Alhamdulillah"), takbir (saying "Allahu akbar"), and tawhid, or by hearing such remembrance from others. God, glorified is He, has called the Qur'an a remembrance, saying: ﴿And this is a blessed remembrance which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya: 50], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, when God alone is mentioned, they believe in Him without doubt, unlike the one described by His words: ﴿And when God alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink﴾ [al-Zumar: 45]. It was also said: their hearts find rest in the Oneness of God. It was also said: the intended "remembrance" here is obedience; it was also said: the promise of God; it was also said: swearing by God, so when his opponent swears by God, his heart is at rest; it was also said: the remembrance of His mercy; it was also said: the remembrance of His signs which indicate His oneness. Indeed, it is only by the remembrance of God alone, and not any other, that hearts find rest. Contemplation of God's creatures and the marvels of His making, although it gives some tranquillity in general, is not like this tranquillity; likewise contemplation of miracles, which are among matters that humans cannot bear, does not produce tranquillity in the way the remembrance of God does. This is the sense of the restrictive construction (qasr) conveyed by this structure.

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds: for them is ṭūbā and a good return﴾. The relative pronoun is the subject, and its predicate is the supplicatory sentence "ṭūbā lahum" according to the well-known interpretation. It is also permissible that the relative clause be in the accusative by way of praise, with "ṭūbā lahum" as the predicate of an omitted subject. It is also permissible that the relative clause be a substitute for "qulūb" (hearts), with an omitted genitive, i.e., "the hearts of those who believe."

Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Zajjaj, and the lexicographers said: ṭūbā is fu'lā from al-ṭayyib (the good).

Ibn al-Anbari said: its interpretation is "the pleasant state." It was also said: ṭūbā is a tree in Paradise; it was also said: it is Paradise itself; it was also said: it is a garden in the Indian language; it was also said: the meaning of "ṭūbā lahum" is "fair end for them"; it was also said: "good for them"; it was also said: "honour for them"; it was also said: "joy for them." Al-Nahhas said: these sayings are close in meaning, and the original form is ṭuybā, the yā' became wāw because of its sukūn and the damma before it. The lām in "lahum" is for clarification, like "saqyan laka" and "ra'yan laka."

"Husn ma'ab" (good return) has also been read in the accusative and the nominative, from "āba" when he returned, i.e., "and a good place of return," which is the Hereafter.

﴿Thus We have sent you to a community before which other communities have passed away﴾, meaning: just as that great sending which includes the dazzling miracle, We have sent you, O Muhammad. It was also said: the favour upon those to whom Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, was sent is likened to the favour upon those to whom the prophets before him were sent. The meaning of "in a community before which other communities have passed away" is: in a generation after which generations have passed, or among a group of people after which groups have passed. ﴿That you may recite to them what We have revealed to you﴾, i.e., that you may read the Qur'an to them, while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful, i.e., the One abounding in mercy toward His servants. Among His mercy to them is the sending of messengers to them and the sending down of books upon them, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 107]. The clause "Say: He is my Lord" is a resumptive sentence, as if they had asked, "And what is the Most Merciful?" So He, glorified is He, said: say, O Muhammad: He is my Lord, i.e., my Creator; there is no god but He, i.e., none deserves worship or faith other than Him. "In Him I have put my trust" in all my affairs, and "to Him" and not to another "is my return" (matāb), i.e., my repentance. In this there is an allusion to the disbelievers and an exhortation for them to return to God and repent from disbelief and enter Islam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit concerning His saying: ﴿And the worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is but an enjoyment﴾ that he said: it is like the provision of a shepherd, whose family gives him a handful of dates, or some flour, or something with which he drinks milk.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse that he said: In the earlier times a man would go out with his camels or his sheep, and he would say to his family, "Give me enjoyment," and they would give him a piece of bread or dates. This is a parable God struck for the world.

al-Tirmidhi reported and graded it sound from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, slept on a mat, and when he rose there was a mark on his side. We said: 'O Messenger of God, should we not make a bed for you?' He said: 'What have I to do with the world? I am in this world only like a rider who took shade under a tree, then went on and left it.'"

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah reported from al-Mustawrid who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "The world compared with the Hereafter is only like what one of you dips his finger into the sea—let him see with what it returns." And he pointed with the index finger.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And their hearts find rest in the remembrance of God﴾ that he said: they turned to it and found comfort in it.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi concerning the verse that he said: when he swears to them by God, they believe him. ﴿Surely by the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾, he said: they become calm.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: "With Muhammad and his companions."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Anas who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said to his companions when this verse was revealed, ﴿Surely by the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾: Do you know what this means? They said: God and His Messenger know best. He said: 'Whoever loves God and His Messenger, and loves my companions.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from 'Ali that "when this verse was revealed, ﴿Surely by the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: That is whoever loves God and His Messenger, and loves the people of my house truthfully and not falsely, and loves the believers present and absent. Surely by the remembrance of God do they love one another."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Ṭūbā lahum﴾ that he said: joy and coolness of the eye.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ikrimah concerning His saying: ﴿Ṭūbā lahum﴾ that he said: "How excellent is what is theirs."

Similar sayings to those we have mentioned have been related from a group of the early scholars, and the preferred interpretation of the verse is that which has been related as a raised (marfu') report to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, as reported by Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi from Utbah ibn 'Abd: "A Bedouin came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, and said: 'O Messenger of God, is there fruit in Paradise?' He said: 'Yes, in it is a tree called Ṭūbā'…" the hadith.

Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban and al-Khatib in his History reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, that "a man said: 'O Messenger of God, ṭūbā for whoever sees you and believes in you.' He said: 'Ṭūbā for whoever believes in me and sees me; then ṭūbā, then ṭūbā, then ṭūbā for whoever believes in me without seeing me.' A man said: 'And what is ṭūbā?' He said: 'A tree in Paradise, a journey of a hundred years; the garments of the people of Paradise come out of its calyxes.'" There are hadiths and reports from the early scholars on this subject. It is also firmly established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Anas who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: 'In Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider travels for a hundred years. Recite if you wish: ﴿And extended shade﴾' [al-Waqi'ah: 30]." In some wordings it is said that it is the Tree of Eternity.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi concerning ﴿And a good return﴾ that he said: "a good turning-place."

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak something similar. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾ that he said: "It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, at the time of Hudaybiyah when he made peace with Quraysh, wrote in the document: 'In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.' Quraysh said: 'As for the Most Merciful, we do not know Him.' The people of the Jahiliyyah used to write: 'In your name, O God.' His companions said: 'Let us fight them.' He said: 'No, but write as they wish.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj something similar concerning this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid concerning ﴿And to Him is my return﴾ that he said: "my repentance."

(p-732).
His saying: ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set in motion﴾. It was said: this is connected to His saying: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. A group of the disbelievers asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to set the mountains of Makkah in motion so that the land would be widened, for it was a narrow land. God, glorified be He, commanded him to answer them with this reply, which contains an exaltation of the status of the Qur'an and a condemnation of the disbelievers' opinion, since they were not content with it and persisted in their obstinacy and in demanding what, if God were to do it, would leave no room for the divine wisdom's requirement of not sending down the signs by which all the servants would believe.

The meaning of ﴿set in motion by it the mountains﴾ is: by its being sent down and recited, they would move from their places of rest. ﴿Or the earth is cut asunder by it﴾, that is, split apart until it becomes scattered pieces. ﴿Or the dead are addressed by it﴾, that is, they become living by its recitation to them, so that they would understand it when they are addressed with it, just as the living understand it.

There has been disagreement about what the response of (لَوْ) (law, "if") is. Al-Farra' said: it is omitted, and its estimate is: "the Qur'an would be this." It is narrated from him that he said: the response is "they would disbelieve in the Most Merciful" (لَكَفَرُوا بِالرَّحْمَنِ), that is, if this were done to them, they would disbelieve in the Most Merciful. It was also said: its response is "they would not believe" (لَما آمَنُوا), as already mentioned in His saying ﴿They would not believe unless God wills﴾ [al-An'am: 111]. It was also said: the response is placed earlier, and in the speech there is a preposing and postposing, that is: "And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful, if only there were a Qur'an..." to the end of it. The Arabs often omit the response of (لَوْ) when the context of the speech indicates it. Among that is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Had it been a soul that dies all together,
But it is a soul that brings down souls."

That is: it would have been easy for me in that case.

﴿Rather, to God belongs the affair entirely﴾. That is: if a Qur'an had been made to do that, this Qur'an would have been it. But it was not done; rather, what is the case now was done. So if He willed that they believe, they would believe; and if He does not will that they believe, the moving of the mountains and all the other signs they proposed would not benefit. Thus the turning away (al-idrab, the "rather") is directed to what the affair belonging to God, glorified be He, leads to and necessitates: that the affair depends on what His wisdom and will require. What indicates that this is the intended meaning is His saying: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired that, if God willed, He would have guided all the people?﴾ Al-Farra' said: al-Kalbi said: "Have not those who believe despaired" means "Have not those who believe known," and this is the dialect of al-Nakha'.

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it says: it was also said that it is the dialect of Hawazin, and a group of the early generations said this. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Have they not known and become clear?"

Al-Zajjaj said: this is a metaphor, because one who despairs of a thing knows that it will not happen. Its parallel is the use of "hope" (raja') to mean "fear" and "forgetting" (nisyan) to mean "abandoning," because each of these two includes the other. This is supported by the recitation of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and a group: "Have they not become clear?" (afalam yatabayyan). From this is the saying of Rabah ibn 'Adi:

"Have not the peoples despaired that I am his son,
Even though I am far from the land of my tribe?"

That is: "Have they not known?" Abu 'Ubayda cited in this the saying of Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nadri:

"I say to them in the mountain pass when they capture me,
'Have you not despaired that I am the son of Faris Zahdam?'"

That is: "Have you not known?" So the meaning of the verse according to this is: "Have not those who believe known that, if God willed, He would have guided all the people, without their having to witness the signs?"

It was also said that "despair" (al-iyas) is in its real meaning, that is: "Have not those who believe despaired of the faith of these disbelievers, because they know that God, exalted be He, if He wanted to guide them, would have guided them?" Because the believers wished for the sending down of the signs that the disbelievers proposed, out of hope for their faith.

﴿And calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieve because of what they have done﴾. This is a warning to the disbelievers in general, or to the disbelievers of Makkah in particular. That is: calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieved, because of what they did of disbelief and denial of the messengers. "Calamity" (qari'a) means a striking misfortune that surprises them. It is said: "qara'ahu al-amr" when the matter struck him. The plural is qawari'. The original meaning of qar' is striking.

The poet said:

"It has consumed my old wealth and what I had gathered of property:
The striking of the flagons upon the mouths of the jugs."

The meaning: the disbelievers will not cease to be thus until a destroying calamity strikes them, of killing, or capture, or drought, or the like of punishment. It has been said: al-qari'a is a misfortune, and it was said: the raiding parties and the expeditions. It is not hidden that qari'a is applied to what is more general than that.

﴿Or it settles near their dwelling﴾, so that they are frightened by it and witness from its traces what makes their hearts tremble and their shoulders quake. It was said: the pronoun in "settles" (tahill) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). The meaning: "Or you, O Muhammad, settle near their dwelling, besieging them and seizing their throats," as happened from him (ﷺ) to the people of al-Ta'if.

﴿Until the promise of God comes﴾, and that is their death, or the establishment of the Hour upon them. For when the inevitable promise of God comes, there befalls them of His punishment what is the utmost of severity. It was said: what is meant by "the promise of God" here is His permission to fight the disbelievers. The first is preferable.

﴿Indeed God does not fail the appointment﴾. Whatever His promise has decreed will certainly occur.

﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, so I gave respite to those who disbelieved﴾. The indefiniteness in "messengers" (rusul) is for multiplicity, that is: many messengers. "Imla'" is granting respite, and its verification has already passed in al-A'raf. ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and threat. That is: "So how was My punishment upon these disbelievers who mocked the messengers? I gave them respite, then I seized them."

Then God, glorified be He, asked another question, for rebuke and censure, which runs in the manner of argument against the disbelievers and of exposing their work and disparaging them. He said: ﴿Then is He who stands over every soul﴾. Al-qa'im means the guardian and the one who takes charge of affairs.

He, glorified be He, meant Himself, for He is the one who takes charge of the affairs of His creation, who manages their conditions by their appointed terms and their provisions and the counting of their deeds, over every soul of the souls, whatever it may be. The answer is omitted, that is: "Is one who has this attribute like one who does not have this attribute among your objects of worship, which neither benefit nor harm?"

Al-Farra' said: it is as if the meaning is: "Is He who stands over every soul by what it earns like their partners whom they have taken besides God?" The purpose of the verse is to deny the equality between them. It was said: what is meant by ﴿He who stands over every soul﴾ (p-733) is the angels entrusted with the children of Adam. The first is preferable.

The clause ﴿And they have set up for God partners﴾ is conjoined to the omitted answer, explaining it, or is a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied, that is: "and they have indeed set up." Or it is conjoined to "And messengers were certainly mocked," that is: they mocked and set up. ﴿Say: name them﴾. That is: say, O Muhammad, "You have set up for Him partners, so name them: who are they?" In this there is a rebuke and censure for them, because such a phrase is only said about a despised thing that does not deserve to be paid attention to. So one says: "Name it if you wish," meaning that it is too contemptible to be named.

It was also said: the meaning is "Name them by the names of gods as you claim." That would then be a threat to them.

﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾ That is: "Do you inform God of partners in the earth whom you worship, while He is the one who knows what is in the heavens and the earth?" ﴿Or of an outward saying?﴾ That is: "Or do you name them partners by an outward saying, without there being any reality to it?" It was also said: the meaning is: "Say to them: Do you inform God of something inward that He does not know, or of something outward that He knows?" If they say "something inward that He does not know," they have brought a false claim; and if they say "something outward that He knows," then say to them: "Name them."

So when they name al-Lat and al-'Uzza and the like, say to them: "God does not know for Himself a partner." He specified the earth in the denial of partners from it, though He has no partner in other than the earth, because they claimed for Him a partner on earth.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿or of an outward saying﴾ is "or of a vain, passing saying," and from it is the saying of the poet:

"You reproached us for their milk and their flesh,
And that is shame, O son of Rayta, manifest."

That is: passing, vain. It was also said: "by a lie of speech." It was also said: the meaning of ﴿of an outward saying﴾ is "by an evident argument of speech according to their claim."

﴿Rather, the scheming of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them﴾. That is: there is no partner for God; rather, the scheming of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them.

Ibn 'Abbas read "zayyana" (with the verb active), so that what made that attractive to them is their scheming. The rest read it in the passive, and the one who makes it attractive is God, glorified be He, or Satan. It is permissible to call the scheming "disbelief," because their scheming against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was disbelief. As for its real meaning, it is deceit, or embellishing with falsehoods.

﴿And they were barred from the way﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read "sudd" (passive), that is: God barred them, or Satan barred them. The rest read it in the active, that is: they barred others. Abu Hatim chose this recitation. Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra on the sad (ṣuddu), "And whomever God leads astray, for him there is no guide," that is: He makes him astray, and His will requires his misguidance, so for him there is no guide who would guide him to good.

The majority read "hadin" without the yā' (of the nominative), according to the common and eloquent dialect. It has been recited with the yā' according to the rare dialect.

Then God, glorified be He, made clear what they deserve, and said: ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾, by what they suffer of killing and capture and other than that. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾ upon them than the punishment of the life of this world. ﴿And they have from God no protector﴾, who would protect them from His punishment, and no defender who would shield them from it.

Then, when God, glorified be He, mentioned what the disbelievers deserve of punishment in the first and the last, He mentioned what He has prepared for the believers, and said: ﴿The description of Paradise which the righteous have been promised: beneath it rivers flow﴾. That is: its wondrous attribute, which in strangeness is like a parable. Ibn Qutayba said: "mathal" in the original language is likeness, and then it may come to mean the form and attribute of a thing. One says: "mathkaltu laka kadha," meaning: I depicted and described it for you. So here by "the description of Paradise" he meant its form and attribute. Then he mentioned it, saying: ﴿beneath it rivers flow﴾, which is like an explanation of "the description."

Sibawayh said: its estimate is "in what We have related to you, the description of Paradise."

Al-Khalil and others said: "the description of Paradise" is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "flow" (tajri).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is an analogy of the unseen by the seen, and its meaning is: "The description of Paradise is a paradise beneath which rivers flow." It was said: the benefit of the predicate returns to ﴿its fruit is constant﴾, that is, it does not cease. Its parallel is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 33].

Al-Farra' said: "mathal" is inserted for emphasis, and the meaning is: "The Paradise which the righteous have been promised, beneath it rivers flow." The Arabs do this often. ﴿And its shade﴾, that is, likewise, constant, not contracting, and the sun does not abrogate it.

The reference in His saying ﴿That﴾ is to the Paradise described with the attributes mentioned earlier, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿the final outcome of those who were righteous﴾, that is, the outcome of those who were wary of disobedience and their final end. ﴿And the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾; they have no outcome nor end except that.

Al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "They said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If it is as you say, then show us our forefathers of the dead, the first ones, that we may speak to them, and widen for us these mountains, the mountains of Makkah, which have constricted us.' So there was revealed: ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set in motion﴾," to the end of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfi, who said: "They said to Muhammad (ﷺ): 'If you would set the mountains of Makkah in motion for us, so that they become spacious and we can plough in them; or if you would cut the earth into sections for us as Sulayman used to divide the land for his people by the wind; or if you would revive the dead for us as ʿIsa used to revive the dead for his people.' So God revealed: ﴿Even if a Qur'an had been by which mountains were moved…﴾ up to His words ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾." He said: "[It means:] Have not those who believe become certain?" They asked: "Do you narrate this hadith from any of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "From Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded it, saying: Abu Zurʿah narrated to us, saying: Minjab ibn al-Harith narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn ʿUmarah informed us, saying: ʿUmar ibn Hassan narrated to us, from ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfi, and he mentioned it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded through al-ʿAwfi, from Ibn ʿAbbas, something similar to it, in abridged form.

Abu Yaʿla, Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, in mentioning the occasion of revelation of the verse, something similar to what has preceded, in a more extended form.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Rather, the command belongs entirely to God﴾: "He does not bring about any of that except what He wills, and He would not have done it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾: "It means: Have they not known?"

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from another route from him, something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Zayd, something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Abu al-ʿAliyah regarding ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾: "Those who believe have despaired that they could guide [the people]; yet had God willed, He would have guided all of mankind."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿A calamity will continue to strike them for what they have done﴾: "[It means] the expeditions."

al-Tayalisi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il recorded from him something similar, and added ﴿Or it descends close to their homes﴾. He said: "You, O Muhammad, until the promise of God comes." He said: "[The promise is] the conquest of Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Saʿid something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿calamity﴾ that he said: "A disaster."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from al-ʿAwfi, from him, regarding ﴿calamity﴾ that he said: "A punishment from the sky." And regarding ﴿Or it descends close to their homes﴾: "meaning the arrival of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) among them and his fighting against their fathers."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also recorded from him, regarding His words ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned…﴾: "He means by that Himself."

(p-732).
His saying: ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set in motion﴾. It was said: this is connected to His saying: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. A group of the disbelievers asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to set the mountains of Makkah in motion so that the land would be widened, for it was a narrow land. God, glorified be He, commanded him to answer them with this reply, which contains an exaltation of the status of the Qur'an and a condemnation of the disbelievers' opinion, since they were not content with it and persisted in their obstinacy and in demanding what, if God were to do it, would leave no room for the divine wisdom's requirement of not sending down the signs by which all the servants would believe.

The meaning of ﴿set in motion by it the mountains﴾ is: by its being sent down and recited, they would move from their places of rest. ﴿Or the earth is cut asunder by it﴾, that is, split apart until it becomes scattered pieces. ﴿Or the dead are addressed by it﴾, that is, they become living by its recitation to them, so that they would understand it when they are addressed with it, just as the living understand it.

There has been disagreement about what the response of (لَوْ) (law, "if") is. Al-Farra' said: it is omitted, and its estimate is: "the Qur'an would be this." It is narrated from him that he said: the response is "they would disbelieve in the Most Merciful" (لَكَفَرُوا بِالرَّحْمَنِ), that is, if this were done to them, they would disbelieve in the Most Merciful. It was also said: its response is "they would not believe" (لَما آمَنُوا), as already mentioned in His saying ﴿They would not believe unless God wills﴾ [al-An'am: 111]. It was also said: the response is placed earlier, and in the speech there is a preposing and postposing, that is: "And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful, if only there were a Qur'an..." to the end of it. The Arabs often omit the response of (لَوْ) when the context of the speech indicates it. Among that is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Had it been a soul that dies all together,
But it is a soul that brings down souls."

That is: it would have been easy for me in that case.

﴿Rather, to God belongs the affair entirely﴾. That is: if a Qur'an had been made to do that, this Qur'an would have been it. But it was not done; rather, what is the case now was done. So if He willed that they believe, they would believe; and if He does not will that they believe, the moving of the mountains and all the other signs they proposed would not benefit. Thus the turning away (al-idrab, the "rather") is directed to what the affair belonging to God, glorified be He, leads to and necessitates: that the affair depends on what His wisdom and will require. What indicates that this is the intended meaning is His saying: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired that, if God willed, He would have guided all the people?﴾ Al-Farra' said: al-Kalbi said: "Have not those who believe despaired" means "Have not those who believe known," and this is the dialect of al-Nakha'.

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it says: it was also said that it is the dialect of Hawazin, and a group of the early generations said this. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Have they not known and become clear?"

Al-Zajjaj said: this is a metaphor, because one who despairs of a thing knows that it will not happen. Its parallel is the use of "hope" (raja') to mean "fear" and "forgetting" (nisyan) to mean "abandoning," because each of these two includes the other. This is supported by the recitation of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and a group: "Have they not become clear?" (afalam yatabayyan). From this is the saying of Rabah ibn 'Adi:

"Have not the peoples despaired that I am his son,
Even though I am far from the land of my tribe?"

That is: "Have they not known?" Abu 'Ubayda cited in this the saying of Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nadri:

"I say to them in the mountain pass when they capture me,
'Have you not despaired that I am the son of Faris Zahdam?'"

That is: "Have you not known?" So the meaning of the verse according to this is: "Have not those who believe known that, if God willed, He would have guided all the people, without their having to witness the signs?"

It was also said that "despair" (al-iyas) is in its real meaning, that is: "Have not those who believe despaired of the faith of these disbelievers, because they know that God, exalted be He, if He wanted to guide them, would have guided them?" Because the believers wished for the sending down of the signs that the disbelievers proposed, out of hope for their faith.

﴿And calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieve because of what they have done﴾. This is a warning to the disbelievers in general, or to the disbelievers of Makkah in particular. That is: calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieved, because of what they did of disbelief and denial of the messengers. "Calamity" (qari'a) means a striking misfortune that surprises them. It is said: "qara'ahu al-amr" when the matter struck him. The plural is qawari'. The original meaning of qar' is striking.

The poet said:

"It has consumed my old wealth and what I had gathered of property:
The striking of the flagons upon the mouths of the jugs."

The meaning: the disbelievers will not cease to be thus until a destroying calamity strikes them, of killing, or capture, or drought, or the like of punishment. It has been said: al-qari'a is a misfortune, and it was said: the raiding parties and the expeditions. It is not hidden that qari'a is applied to what is more general than that.

﴿Or it settles near their dwelling﴾, so that they are frightened by it and witness from its traces what makes their hearts tremble and their shoulders quake. It was said: the pronoun in "settles" (tahill) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). The meaning: "Or you, O Muhammad, settle near their dwelling, besieging them and seizing their throats," as happened from him (ﷺ) to the people of al-Ta'if.

﴿Until the promise of God comes﴾, and that is their death, or the establishment of the Hour upon them. For when the inevitable promise of God comes, there befalls them of His punishment what is the utmost of severity. It was said: what is meant by "the promise of God" here is His permission to fight the disbelievers. The first is preferable.

﴿Indeed God does not fail the appointment﴾. Whatever His promise has decreed will certainly occur.

﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, so I gave respite to those who disbelieved﴾. The indefiniteness in "messengers" (rusul) is for multiplicity, that is: many messengers. "Imla'" is granting respite, and its verification has already passed in al-A'raf. ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and threat. That is: "So how was My punishment upon these disbelievers who mocked the messengers? I gave them respite, then I seized them."

Then God, glorified be He, asked another question, for rebuke and censure, which runs in the manner of argument against the disbelievers and of exposing their work and disparaging them. He said: ﴿Then is He who stands over every soul﴾. Al-qa'im means the guardian and the one who takes charge of affairs.

He, glorified be He, meant Himself, for He is the one who takes charge of the affairs of His creation, who manages their conditions by their appointed terms and their provisions and the counting of their deeds, over every soul of the souls, whatever it may be. The answer is omitted, that is: "Is one who has this attribute like one who does not have this attribute among your objects of worship, which neither benefit nor harm?"

Al-Farra' said: it is as if the meaning is: "Is He who stands over every soul by what it earns like their partners whom they have taken besides God?" The purpose of the verse is to deny the equality between them. It was said: what is meant by ﴿He who stands over every soul﴾ (p-733) is the angels entrusted with the children of Adam. The first is preferable.

The clause ﴿And they have set up for God partners﴾ is conjoined to the omitted answer, explaining it, or is a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied, that is: "and they have indeed set up." Or it is conjoined to "And messengers were certainly mocked," that is: they mocked and set up. ﴿Say: name them﴾. That is: say, O Muhammad, "You have set up for Him partners, so name them: who are they?" In this there is a rebuke and censure for them, because such a phrase is only said about a despised thing that does not deserve to be paid attention to. So one says: "Name it if you wish," meaning that it is too contemptible to be named.

It was also said: the meaning is "Name them by the names of gods as you claim." That would then be a threat to them.

﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾ That is: "Do you inform God of partners in the earth whom you worship, while He is the one who knows what is in the heavens and the earth?" ﴿Or of an outward saying?﴾ That is: "Or do you name them partners by an outward saying, without there being any reality to it?" It was also said: the meaning is: "Say to them: Do you inform God of something inward that He does not know, or of something outward that He knows?" If they say "something inward that He does not know," they have brought a false claim; and if they say "something outward that He knows," then say to them: "Name them."

So when they name al-Lat and al-'Uzza and the like, say to them: "God does not know for Himself a partner." He specified the earth in the denial of partners from it, though He has no partner in other than the earth, because they claimed for Him a partner on earth.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿or of an outward saying﴾ is "or of a vain, passing saying," and from it is the saying of the poet:

"You reproached us for their milk and their flesh,
And that is shame, O son of Rayta, manifest."

That is: passing, vain. It was also said: "by a lie of speech." It was also said: the meaning of ﴿of an outward saying﴾ is "by an evident argument of speech according to their claim."

﴿Rather, the scheming of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them﴾. That is: there is no partner for God; rather, the scheming of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them.

Ibn 'Abbas read "zayyana" (with the verb active), so that what made that attractive to them is their scheming. The rest read it in the passive, and the one who makes it attractive is God, glorified be He, or Satan. It is permissible to call the scheming "disbelief," because their scheming against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was disbelief. As for its real meaning, it is deceit, or embellishing with falsehoods.

﴿And they were barred from the way﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read "sudd" (passive), that is: God barred them, or Satan barred them. The rest read it in the active, that is: they barred others. Abu Hatim chose this recitation. Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra on the sad (ṣuddu), "And whomever God leads astray, for him there is no guide," that is: He makes him astray, and His will requires his misguidance, so for him there is no guide who would guide him to good.

The majority read "hadin" without the yā' (of the nominative), according to the common and eloquent dialect. It has been recited with the yā' according to the rare dialect.

Then God, glorified be He, made clear what they deserve, and said: ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾, by what they suffer of killing and capture and other than that. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾ upon them than the punishment of the life of this world. ﴿And they have from God no protector﴾, who would protect them from His punishment, and no defender who would shield them from it.

Then, when God, glorified be He, mentioned what the disbelievers deserve of punishment in the first and the last, He mentioned what He has prepared for the believers, and said: ﴿The description of Paradise which the righteous have been promised: beneath it rivers flow﴾. That is: its wondrous attribute, which in strangeness is like a parable. Ibn Qutayba said: "mathal" in the original language is likeness, and then it may come to mean the form and attribute of a thing. One says: "mathkaltu laka kadha," meaning: I depicted and described it for you. So here by "the description of Paradise" he meant its form and attribute. Then he mentioned it, saying: ﴿beneath it rivers flow﴾, which is like an explanation of "the description."

Sibawayh said: its estimate is "in what We have related to you, the description of Paradise."

Al-Khalil and others said: "the description of Paradise" is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "flow" (tajri).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is an analogy of the unseen by the seen, and its meaning is: "The description of Paradise is a paradise beneath which rivers flow." It was said: the benefit of the predicate returns to ﴿its fruit is constant﴾, that is, it does not cease. Its parallel is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 33].

Al-Farra' said: "mathal" is inserted for emphasis, and the meaning is: "The Paradise which the righteous have been promised, beneath it rivers flow." The Arabs do this often. ﴿And its shade﴾, that is, likewise, constant, not contracting, and the sun does not abrogate it.

The reference in His saying ﴿That﴾ is to the Paradise described with the attributes mentioned earlier, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿the final outcome of those who were righteous﴾, that is, the outcome of those who were wary of disobedience and their final end. ﴿And the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾; they have no outcome nor end except that.

Al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "They said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If it is as you say, then show us our forefathers of the dead, the first ones, that we may speak to them, and widen for us these mountains, the mountains of Makkah, which have constricted us.' So there was revealed: ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set in motion﴾," to the end of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfi, who said: "They said to Muhammad (ﷺ): 'If you would set the mountains of Makkah in motion for us, so that they become spacious and we can plough in them; or if you would cut the earth into sections for us as Sulayman used to divide the land for his people by the wind; or if you would revive the dead for us as ʿIsa used to revive the dead for his people.' So God revealed: ﴿Even if a Qur'an had been by which mountains were moved…﴾ up to His words ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾." He said: "[It means:] Have not those who believe become certain?" They asked: "Do you narrate this hadith from any of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "From Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ)."

﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, so I gave respite to those who disbelieved﴾. The indefiniteness in "messengers" (rusul) is for multiplicity, that is: many messengers. "Imla'" is granting respite, and its verification has already passed in al-A'raf. ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and threat. That is: "So how was My punishment upon these disbelievers who mocked the messengers? I gave them respite, then I seized them."

Then God, glorified be He, asked another question, for rebuke and censure, which runs in the manner of argument against the disbelievers and of exposing their work and disparaging them. He said: ﴿Then is He who stands over every soul﴾. Al-qa'im means the guardian and the one who takes charge of affairs.

He, glorified be He, meant Himself, for He is the one who takes charge of the affairs of His creation, who manages their conditions by their appointed terms and their provisions and the counting of their deeds, over every soul of the souls, whatever it may be. The answer is omitted, that is: "Is one who has this attribute like one who does not have this attribute among your objects of worship, which neither benefit nor harm?"

Al-Farra' said: it is as if the meaning is: "Is He who stands over every soul by what it earns like their partners whom they have taken besides God?" The purpose of the verse is to deny the equality between them. It was said: what is meant by ﴿He who stands over every soul﴾ (p-733) is the angels entrusted with the children of Adam. The first is preferable.

The clause ﴿And they have set up for God partners﴾ is conjoined to the omitted answer, explaining it, or is a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied, that is: "and they have indeed set up." Or it is conjoined to "And messengers were certainly mocked," that is: they mocked and set up. ﴿Say: name them﴾. That is: say, O Muhammad, "You have set up for Him partners, so name them: who are they?" In this there is a rebuke and censure for them, because such a phrase is only said about a despised thing that does not deserve to be paid attention to. So one says: "Name it if you wish," meaning that it is too contemptible to be named.

It was also said: the meaning is "Name them by the names of gods as you claim." That would then be a threat to them.

﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾ That is: "Do you inform God of partners in the earth whom you worship, while He is the one who knows what is in the heavens and the earth?" ﴿Or of an outward saying?﴾ That is: "Or do you name them partners by an outward saying, without there being any reality to it?" It was also said: the meaning is: "Say to them: Do you inform God of something inward that He does not know, or of something outward that He knows?" If they say "something inward that He does not know," they have brought a false claim; and if they say "something outward that He knows," then say to them: "Name them."

So when they name al-Lat and al-'Uzza and the like, say to them: "God does not know for Himself a partner." He specified the earth in the denial of partners from it, though He has no partner in other than the earth, because they claimed for Him a partner on earth.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿or of an outward saying﴾ is "or of a vain, passing saying," and from it is the saying of the poet:

"You reproached us for their milk and their flesh,
And that is shame, O son of Rayta, manifest."

That is: passing, vain. It was also said: "by a lie of speech." It was also said: the meaning of ﴿of an outward saying﴾ is "by an evident argument of speech according to their claim."

﴿Rather, the scheming of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them﴾. That is: there is no partner for God; rather, the scheming of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them.

Ibn 'Abbas read "zayyana" (with the verb active), so that what made that attractive to them is their scheming. The rest read it in the passive, and the one who makes it attractive is God, glorified be He, or Satan. It is permissible to call the scheming "disbelief," because their scheming against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was disbelief. As for its real meaning, it is deceit, or embellishing with falsehoods.

﴿And they were barred from the way﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read "sudd" (passive), that is: God barred them, or Satan barred them. The rest read it in the active, that is: they barred others. Abu Hatim chose this recitation. Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra on the sad (ṣuddu), "And whomever God leads astray, for him there is no guide," that is: He makes him astray, and His will requires his misguidance, so for him there is no guide who would guide him to good.

The majority read "hadin" without the yā' (of the nominative), according to the common and eloquent dialect. It has been recited with the yā' according to the rare dialect.

Then God, glorified be He, made clear what they deserve, and said: ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾, by what they suffer of killing and capture and other than that. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾ upon them than the punishment of the life of this world. ﴿And they have from God no protector﴾, who would protect them from His punishment, and no defender who would shield them from it.

Then, when God, glorified be He, mentioned what the disbelievers deserve of punishment in the first and the last, He mentioned what He has prepared for the believers, and said: ﴿The description of Paradise which the righteous have been promised: beneath it rivers flow﴾. That is: its wondrous attribute, which in strangeness is like a parable. Ibn Qutayba said: "mathal" in the original language is likeness, and then it may come to mean the form and attribute of a thing. One says: "mathkaltu laka kadha," meaning: I depicted and described it for you. So here by "the description of Paradise" he meant its form and attribute. Then he mentioned it, saying: ﴿beneath it rivers flow﴾, which is like an explanation of "the description."

Sibawayh said: its estimate is "in what We have related to you, the description of Paradise."

Al-Khalil and others said: "the description of Paradise" is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "flow" (tajri).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is an analogy of the unseen by the seen, and its meaning is: "The description of Paradise is a paradise beneath which rivers flow." It was said: the benefit of the predicate returns to ﴿its fruit is constant﴾, that is, it does not cease. Its parallel is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 33].

Al-Farra' said: "mathal" is inserted for emphasis, and the meaning is: "The Paradise which the righteous have been promised, beneath it rivers flow." The Arabs do this often. ﴿And its shade﴾, that is, likewise, constant, not contracting, and the sun does not abrogate it.

The reference in His saying ﴿That﴾ is to the Paradise described with the attributes mentioned earlier, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿the final outcome of those who were righteous﴾, that is, the outcome of those who were wary of disobedience and their final end. ﴿And the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾; they have no outcome nor end except that.

Al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "They said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If it is as you say, then show us our forefathers of the dead, the first ones, that we may speak to them, and widen for us these mountains, the mountains of Makkah, which have constricted us.' So there was revealed: ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set in motion﴾," to the end of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfi, who said: "They said to Muhammad (ﷺ): 'If you would set the mountains of Makkah in motion for us, so that they become spacious and we can plough in them; or if you would cut the earth into sections for us as Sulayman used to divide the land for his people by the wind; or if you would revive the dead for us as ʿIsa used to revive the dead for his people.' So God revealed: ﴿Even if a Qur'an had been by which mountains were moved…﴾ up to His words ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾." He said: "[It means:] Have not those who believe become certain?" They asked: "Do you narrate this hadith from any of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "From Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded it, saying: Abu Zurʿah narrated to us, saying: Minjab ibn al-Harith narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn ʿUmarah informed us, saying: ʿUmar ibn Hassan narrated to us, from ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfi, and he mentioned it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded through al-ʿAwfi, from Ibn ʿAbbas, something similar to it, in abridged form.

Abu Yaʿla, Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, in mentioning the occasion of revelation of the verse, something similar to what has preceded, in a more extended form.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Rather, the command belongs entirely to God﴾: "He does not bring about any of that except what He wills, and He would not have done it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾: "It means: Have they not known?"

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from another route from him, something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Zayd, something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Abu al-ʿAliyah regarding ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾: "Those who believe have despaired that they could guide [the people]; yet had God willed, He would have guided all of mankind."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿A calamity will continue to strike them for what they have done﴾: "[It means] the expeditions."

al-Tayalisi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il recorded from him something similar, and added ﴿Or it descends close to their homes﴾. He said: "You, O Muhammad, until the promise of God comes." He said: "[The promise is] the conquest of Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Saʿid something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿calamity﴾ that he said: "A disaster."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from al-ʿAwfi, from him, regarding ﴿calamity﴾ that he said: "A punishment from the sky." And regarding ﴿Or it descends close to their homes﴾: "meaning the arrival of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) among them and his fighting against their fathers."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also recorded from him, regarding His words ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned…﴾: "He means by that Himself."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from ʿAṭa' regarding the verse: "God, the Exalted, stands over every soul in justice and fairness."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿Or with an apparent speech﴾: "The apparent speech is falsehood."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from ʿIkrimah regarding His words ﴿The description of Paradise﴾: "The attribute of Paradise; Paradise has no likeness."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibrahim al-Taymi regarding His words ﴿Its fruit is constant﴾: "Its pleasures are constant in their mouths."

(p-732).
His saying: ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set in motion﴾. It was said: this is connected to His saying: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. A group of the disbelievers asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to set the mountains of Makkah in motion so that the land would be widened, for it was a narrow land. God, glorified be He, commanded him to answer them with this reply, which contains an exaltation of the status of the Qur'an and a condemnation of the disbelievers' opinion, since they were not content with it and persisted in their obstinacy and in demanding what, if God were to do it, would leave no room for the divine wisdom's requirement of not sending down the signs by which all the servants would believe.

The meaning of ﴿set in motion by it the mountains﴾ is: by its being sent down and recited, they would move from their places of rest. ﴿Or the earth is cut asunder by it﴾, that is, split apart until it becomes scattered pieces. ﴿Or the dead are addressed by it﴾, that is, they become living by its recitation to them, so that they would understand it when they are addressed with it, just as the living understand it.

There has been disagreement about what the response of (لَوْ) (law, "if") is. Al-Farra' said: it is omitted, and its estimate is: "the Qur'an would be this." It is narrated from him that he said: the response is "they would disbelieve in the Most Merciful" (لَكَفَرُوا بِالرَّحْمَنِ), that is, if this were done to them, they would disbelieve in the Most Merciful. It was also said: its response is "they would not believe" (لَما آمَنُوا), as already mentioned in His saying ﴿They would not believe unless God wills﴾ [al-An'am: 111]. It was also said: the response is placed earlier, and in the speech there is a preposing and postposing, that is: "And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful, if only there were a Qur'an..." to the end of it. The Arabs often omit the response of (لَوْ) when the context of the speech indicates it. Among that is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Had it been a soul that dies all together,
But it is a soul that brings down souls."

That is: it would have been easy for me in that case.

﴿Rather, to God belongs the affair entirely﴾. That is: if a Qur'an had been made to do that, this Qur'an would have been it. But it was not done; rather, what is the case now was done. So if He willed that they believe, they would believe; and if He does not will that they believe, the moving of the mountains and all the other signs they proposed would not benefit. Thus the turning away (al-idrab, the "rather") is directed to what the affair belonging to God, glorified be He, leads to and necessitates: that the affair depends on what His wisdom and will require. What indicates that this is the intended meaning is His saying: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired that, if God willed, He would have guided all the people?﴾ Al-Farra' said: al-Kalbi said: "Have not those who believe despaired" means "Have not those who believe known," and this is the dialect of al-Nakha'.

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it says: it was also said that it is the dialect of Hawazin, and a group of the early generations said this. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Have they not known and become clear?"

Al-Zajjaj said: this is a metaphor, because one who despairs of a thing knows that it will not happen. Its parallel is the use of "hope" (raja') to mean "fear" and "forgetting" (nisyan) to mean "abandoning," because each of these two includes the other. This is supported by the recitation of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and a group: "Have they not become clear?" (afalam yatabayyan). From this is the saying of Rabah ibn 'Adi:

"Have not the peoples despaired that I am his son,
Even though I am far from the land of my tribe?"

That is: "Have they not known?" Abu 'Ubayda cited in this the saying of Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nadri:

"I say to them in the mountain pass when they capture me,
'Have you not despaired that I am the son of Faris Zahdam?'"

That is: "Have you not known?" So the meaning of the verse according to this is: "Have not those who believe known that, if God willed, He would have guided all the people, without their having to witness the signs?"

It was also said that "despair" (al-iyas) is in its real meaning, that is: "Have not those who believe despaired of the faith of these disbelievers, because they know that God, exalted be He, if He wanted to guide them, would have guided them?" Because the believers wished for the sending down of the signs that the disbelievers proposed, out of hope for their faith.

﴿And calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieve because of what they have done﴾. This is a warning to the disbelievers in general, or to the disbelievers of Makkah in particular. That is: calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieved, because of what they did of disbelief and denial of the messengers. "Calamity" (qari'a) means a striking misfortune that surprises them. It is said: "qara'ahu al-amr" when the matter struck him. The plural is qawari'. The original meaning of qar' is striking.

The poet said:

"It has consumed my old wealth and what I had gathered of property:
The striking of the flagons upon the mouths of the jugs."

The meaning: the disbelievers will not cease to be thus until a destroying calamity strikes them, of killing, or capture, or drought, or the like of punishment. It has been said: al-qari'a is a misfortune, and it was said: the raiding parties and the expeditions. It is not hidden that qari'a is applied to what is more general than that.

﴿Or it settles near their dwelling﴾, so that they are frightened by it and witness from its traces what makes their hearts tremble and their shoulders quake. It was said: the pronoun in "settles" (tahill) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). The meaning: "Or you, O Muhammad, settle near their dwelling, besieging them and seizing their throats," as happened from him (ﷺ) to the people of al-Ta'if.

﴿Until the promise of God comes﴾, and that is their death, or the establishment of the Hour upon them. For when the inevitable promise of God comes, there befalls them of His punishment what is the utmost of severity. It was said: what is meant by "the promise of God" here is His permission to fight the disbelievers. The first is preferable.

﴿Indeed God does not fail the appointment﴾. Whatever His promise has decreed will certainly occur.
