He said: "You, O Muhammad, until the promise of God comes." He said: "[The promise is] the conquest of Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Saʿid something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿calamity﴾ that he said: "A disaster."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from al-ʿAwfi, from him, regarding ﴿calamity﴾ that he said: "A punishment from the sky." And regarding ﴿Or it descends close to their homes﴾: "meaning the arrival of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) among them and his fighting against their fathers."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also recorded from him, regarding His words ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned…﴾: "He means by that Himself."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from ʿAṭa' regarding the verse: "God, the Exalted, stands over every soul in justice and fairness."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿Or with an apparent speech﴾: "The apparent speech is falsehood."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from ʿIkrimah regarding His words ﴿The description of Paradise﴾: "The attribute of Paradise; Paradise has no likeness."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibrahim al-Taymi regarding His words ﴿Its fruit is constant﴾: "Its pleasures are constant in their mouths."

(p-732).
His saying: ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set in motion﴾. It was said: this is connected to His saying: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. A group of the disbelievers asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to set the mountains of Makkah in motion so that the land would be widened, for it was a narrow land. God, glorified be He, commanded him to answer them with this reply, which contains an exaltation of the status of the Qur'an and a condemnation of the disbelievers' opinion, since they were not content with it and persisted in their obstinacy and in demanding what, if God were to do it, would leave no room for the divine wisdom's requirement of not sending down the signs by which all the servants would believe.

The meaning of ﴿set in motion by it the mountains﴾ is: by its being sent down and recited, they would move from their places of rest. ﴿Or the earth is cut asunder by it﴾, that is, split apart until it becomes scattered pieces. ﴿Or the dead are addressed by it﴾, that is, they become living by its recitation to them, so that they would understand it when they are addressed with it, just as the living understand it.

There has been disagreement about what the response of (لَوْ) (law, "if") is. Al-Farra' said: it is omitted, and its estimate is: "the Qur'an would be this." It is narrated from him that he said: the response is "they would disbelieve in the Most Merciful" (لَكَفَرُوا بِالرَّحْمَنِ), that is, if this were done to them, they would disbelieve in the Most Merciful. It was also said: its response is "they would not believe" (لَما آمَنُوا), as already mentioned in His saying ﴿They would not believe unless God wills﴾ [al-An'am: 111]. It was also said: the response is placed earlier, and in the speech there is a preposing and postposing, that is: "And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful, if only there were a Qur'an..." to the end of it. The Arabs often omit the response of (لَوْ) when the context of the speech indicates it. Among that is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Had it been a soul that dies all together,
But it is a soul that brings down souls."

That is: it would have been easy for me in that case.

﴿Rather, to God belongs the affair entirely﴾. That is: if a Qur'an had been made to do that, this Qur'an would have been it. But it was not done; rather, what is the case now was done. So if He willed that they believe, they would believe; and if He does not will that they believe, the moving of the mountains and all the other signs they proposed would not benefit. Thus the turning away (al-idrab, the "rather") is directed to what the affair belonging to God, glorified be He, leads to and necessitates: that the affair depends on what His wisdom and will require. What indicates that this is the intended meaning is His saying: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired that, if God willed, He would have guided all the people?﴾ Al-Farra' said: al-Kalbi said: "Have not those who believe despaired" means "Have not those who believe known," and this is the dialect of al-Nakha'.

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it says: it was also said that it is the dialect of Hawazin, and a group of the early generations said this. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Have they not known and become clear?"

Al-Zajjaj said: this is a metaphor, because one who despairs of a thing knows that it will not happen. Its parallel is the use of "hope" (raja') to mean "fear" and "forgetting" (nisyan) to mean "abandoning," because each of these two includes the other. This is supported by the recitation of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and a group: "Have they not become clear?" (afalam yatabayyan). From this is the saying of Rabah ibn 'Adi:

"Have not the peoples despaired that I am his son,
Even though I am far from the land of my tribe?"

That is: "Have they not known?" Abu 'Ubayda cited in this the saying of Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nadri:

"I say to them in the mountain pass when they capture me,
'Have you not despaired that I am the son of Faris Zahdam?'"

That is: "Have you not known?" So the meaning of the verse according to this is: "Have not those who believe known that, if God willed, He would have guided all the people, without their having to witness the signs?"

It was also said that "despair" (al-iyas) is in its real meaning, that is: "Have not those who believe despaired of the faith of these disbelievers, because they know that God, exalted be He, if He wanted to guide them, would have guided them?" Because the believers wished for the sending down of the signs that the disbelievers proposed, out of hope for their faith.

﴿And calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieve because of what they have done﴾. This is a warning to the disbelievers in general, or to the disbelievers of Makkah in particular. That is: calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieved, because of what they did of disbelief and denial of the messengers. "Calamity" (qari'a) means a striking misfortune that surprises them. It is said: "qara'ahu al-amr" when the matter struck him. The plural is qawari'. The original meaning of qar' is striking.

The poet said:

"It has consumed my old wealth and what I had gathered of property:
The striking of the flagons upon the mouths of the jugs."

The meaning: the disbelievers will not cease to be thus until a destroying calamity strikes them, of killing, or capture, or drought, or the like of punishment. It has been said: al-qari'a is a misfortune, and it was said: the raiding parties and the expeditions. It is not hidden that qari'a is applied to what is more general than that.

﴿Or it settles near their dwelling﴾, so that they are frightened by it and witness from its traces what makes their hearts tremble and their shoulders quake. It was said: the pronoun in "settles" (tahill) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). The meaning: "Or you, O Muhammad, settle near their dwelling, besieging them and seizing their throats," as happened from him (ﷺ) to the people of al-Ta'if.

﴿Until the promise of God comes﴾, and that is their death, or the establishment of the Hour upon them. For when the inevitable promise of God comes, there befalls them of His punishment what is the utmost of severity. It was said: what is meant by "the promise of God" here is His permission to fight the disbelievers. The first is preferable.

﴿Indeed God does not fail the appointment﴾. Whatever His promise has decreed will certainly occur.

﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, so I gave respite to those who disbelieved﴾. The indefiniteness in "messengers" (rusul) is for multiplicity, that is: many messengers. "Imla'" is granting respite, and its verification has already passed in al-A'raf. ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and threat. That is: "So how was My punishment upon these disbelievers who mocked the messengers? I gave them respite, then I seized them."

Then God, glorified be He, asked another question, for rebuke and censure, which runs in the manner of argument against the disbelievers and of exposing their work and disparaging them. He said: ﴿Then is He who stands over every soul﴾. Al-qa'im means the guardian and the one who takes charge of affairs.

He, glorified be He, meant Himself, for He is the one who takes charge of the affairs of His creation, who manages their conditions by their appointed terms and their provisions and the counting of their deeds, over every soul of the souls, whatever it may be. The answer is omitted, that is: "Is one who has this attribute like one who does not have this attribute among your objects of worship, which neither benefit nor harm?"

Al-Farra' said: it is as if the meaning is: "Is He who stands over every soul by what it earns like their partners whom they have taken besides God?" The purpose of the verse is to deny the equality between them. It was said: what is meant by ﴿He who stands over every soul﴾ (p-733) is the angels entrusted with the children of Adam. The first is preferable.

The clause ﴿And they have set up for God partners﴾ is conjoined to the omitted answer, explaining it, or is a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied, that is: "and they have indeed set up." Or it is conjoined to "And messengers were certainly mocked," that is: they mocked and set up. ﴿Say: name them﴾. That is: say, O Muhammad, "You have set up for Him partners, so name them: who are they?" In this there is a rebuke and censure for them, because such a phrase is only said about a despised thing that does not deserve to be paid attention to. So one says: "Name it if you wish," meaning that it is too contemptible to be named.

It was also said: the meaning is "Name them by the names of gods as you claim." That would then be a threat to them.

﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾ That is: "Do you inform God of partners in the earth whom you worship, while He is the one who knows what is in the heavens and the earth?" ﴿Or of an outward saying?﴾ That is: "Or do you name them partners by an outward saying, without there being any reality to it?" It was also said: the meaning is: "Say to them: Do you inform God of something inward that He does not know, or of something outward that He knows?" If they say "something inward that He does not know," they have brought a false claim; and if they say "something outward that He knows," then say to them: "Name them."

So when they name al-Lat and al-'Uzza and the like, say to them: "God does not know for Himself a partner." He specified the earth in the denial of partners from it, though He has no partner in other than the earth, because they claimed for Him a partner on earth.

It was also said: the meaning of ﴿or of an outward saying﴾ is "or of a vain, passing saying," and from it is the saying of the poet:

"You reproached us for their milk and their flesh,
And that is shame, O son of Rayta, manifest."

That is: passing, vain. It was also said: "by a lie of speech." It was also said: the meaning of ﴿of an outward saying﴾ is "by an evident argument of speech according to their claim."

﴿Rather, the scheming of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them﴾. That is: there is no partner for God; rather, the scheming of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them.

Ibn 'Abbas read "zayyana" (with the verb active), so that what made that attractive to them is their scheming. The rest read it in the passive, and the one who makes it attractive is God, glorified be He, or Satan. It is permissible to call the scheming "disbelief," because their scheming against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was disbelief. As for its real meaning, it is deceit, or embellishing with falsehoods.

﴿And they were barred from the way﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read "sudd" (passive), that is: God barred them, or Satan barred them. The rest read it in the active, that is: they barred others. Abu Hatim chose this recitation. Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra on the sad (ṣuddu), "And whomever God leads astray, for him there is no guide," that is: He makes him astray, and His will requires his misguidance, so for him there is no guide who would guide him to good.

The majority read "hadin" without the yā' (of the nominative), according to the common and eloquent dialect. It has been recited with the yā' according to the rare dialect.

Then God, glorified be He, made clear what they deserve, and said: ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾, by what they suffer of killing and capture and other than that. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾ upon them than the punishment of the life of this world. ﴿And they have from God no protector﴾, who would protect them from His punishment, and no defender who would shield them from it.

Then, when God, glorified be He, mentioned what the disbelievers deserve of punishment in the first and the last, He mentioned what He has prepared for the believers, and said: ﴿The description of Paradise which the righteous have been promised: beneath it rivers flow﴾. That is: its wondrous attribute, which in strangeness is like a parable. Ibn Qutayba said: "mathal" in the original language is likeness, and then it may come to mean the form and attribute of a thing. One says: "mathkaltu laka kadha," meaning: I depicted and described it for you. So here by "the description of Paradise" he meant its form and attribute. Then he mentioned it, saying: ﴿beneath it rivers flow﴾, which is like an explanation of "the description."

Sibawayh said: its estimate is "in what We have related to you, the description of Paradise."

Al-Khalil and others said: "the description of Paradise" is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "flow" (tajri).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is an analogy of the unseen by the seen, and its meaning is: "The description of Paradise is a paradise beneath which rivers flow." It was said: the benefit of the predicate returns to ﴿its fruit is constant﴾, that is, it does not cease. Its parallel is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 33].

Al-Farra' said: "mathal" is inserted for emphasis, and the meaning is: "The Paradise which the righteous have been promised, beneath it rivers flow." The Arabs do this often. ﴿And its shade﴾, that is, likewise, constant, not contracting, and the sun does not abrogate it.

The reference in His saying ﴿That﴾ is to the Paradise described with the attributes mentioned earlier, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿the final outcome of those who were righteous﴾, that is, the outcome of those who were wary of disobedience and their final end. ﴿And the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾; they have no outcome nor end except that.

Al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "They said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If it is as you say, then show us our forefathers of the dead, the first ones, that we may speak to them, and widen for us these mountains, the mountains of Makkah, which have constricted us.' So there was revealed: ﴿And if only there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be set in motion﴾," to the end of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfi, who said: "They said to Muhammad (ﷺ): 'If you would set the mountains of Makkah in motion for us, so that they become spacious and we can plough in them; or if you would cut the earth into sections for us as Sulayman used to divide the land for his people by the wind; or if you would revive the dead for us as ʿIsa used to revive the dead for his people.' So God revealed: ﴿Even if a Qur'an had been by which mountains were moved…﴾ up to His words ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾." He said: "[It means:] Have not those who believe become certain?" They asked: "Do you narrate this hadith from any of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "From Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded it, saying: Abu Zurʿah narrated to us, saying: Minjab ibn al-Harith narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn ʿUmarah informed us, saying: ʿUmar ibn Hassan narrated to us, from ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfi, and he mentioned it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded through al-ʿAwfi, from Ibn ʿAbbas, something similar to it, in abridged form.

Abu Yaʿla, Abu Nuʿaym in al-Dala'il and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, in mentioning the occasion of revelation of the verse, something similar to what has preceded, in a more extended form.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Rather, the command belongs entirely to God﴾: "He does not bring about any of that except what He wills, and He would not have done it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾: "It means: Have they not known?"

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from another route from him, something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Zayd, something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Abu al-ʿAliyah regarding ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾: "Those who believe have despaired that they could guide [the people]; yet had God willed, He would have guided all of mankind."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿A calamity will continue to strike them for what they have done﴾: "[It means] the expeditions."

al-Tayalisi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il recorded from him something similar, and added ﴿Or it descends close to their homes﴾. He said: "You, O Muhammad, until the promise of God comes." He said: "[The promise is] the conquest of Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Saʿid something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿calamity﴾ that he said: "A disaster."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from al-ʿAwfi, from him, regarding ﴿calamity﴾ that he said: "A punishment from the sky." And regarding ﴿Or it descends close to their homes﴾: "meaning the arrival of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) among them and his fighting against their fathers."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also recorded from him, regarding His words ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned…﴾: "He means by that Himself."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from ʿAṭa' regarding the verse: "God, the Exalted, stands over every soul in justice and fairness."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿Or with an apparent speech﴾: "The apparent speech is falsehood."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from ʿIkrimah regarding His words ﴿The description of Paradise﴾: "The attribute of Paradise; Paradise has no likeness."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibrahim al-Taymi regarding His words ﴿Its fruit is constant﴾: "Its pleasures are constant in their mouths."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 13, verse 36–39 (part 1 of 2):

The commentators differed over the meaning of "the Book" mentioned here. It was said: it is the Torah and the Gospel, and those who rejoice at what has been sent down to the Messenger of God are those among the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam.

It was also said: those who rejoice are the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitabayn), because it agrees with what is in their books and confirms it. According to the first view, the intended meaning of His words, ﴿And among the factions are those who deny part of it﴾, is those among the Jews and Christians who did not embrace Islam. According to the second view, the intended meaning is the polytheists of Mecca and those like them; or it refers to some of the People of the Two Books, that is, of their factions, for they denied it because it contains abrogation of their laws. So the joy of those among them who rejoiced turns toward what agrees with what is in the two Books, and the denial of those among them who denied turns toward what opposes them both.

It was also said: the Book is the Qur'an, those who rejoice in it are the Muslims, and the factions are those who banded together against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from among the polytheists, Jews and Christians. The "part" they deny is whatever opposes what they themselves believe, according to the differences in their beliefs.

This was objected to: the joy of the Muslims at the revelation of the Qur'an is well known, so there is no benefit in mentioning it. It was answered that what is meant is an increase in joy and rejoicing.

Many commentators said: 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and those among the People of the Book who believed with him were distressed by the scarcity of the mention of al-Rahman in the Qur'an, given how often He is mentioned in the Torah. So God sent down ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon al-Rahman﴾ [al-Isra: 110], and they rejoiced at that. Then, when He had explained what the revelation of the Qur'an produces, namely joy for some and denial for others, He stated what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was to say, and commanded him to say it to them. So He said: ﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him﴾, meaning, I do not associate with Him in any way. That is, say to them, O Muhammad, as a establishing of the proof and a rejection of their denial: I have only been commanded, in what has been revealed to me, to worship Allah and to affirm His oneness. This is a matter on which all the revealed laws agree, and on which all the religions that follow the messengers concur in not denying it.

The readers agreed on the accusative of "and not associate with Him" as a conjunction with "worship" (a'budu). Abu Khulayd read it in the nominative as a new sentence, and this reading was transmitted from Nafi'. The meaning would then be: "I call (adu'u) to Allah," that is, to Allah alone and not to other than Him, or to what I have been commanded, which is worshipping Allah alone. The first reading is better, because of His words ﴿and to Him is my return﴾, since the pronoun refers to Allah, glorified is He, meaning: to Him alone, not to other than Him, is my return.

Then He mentioned some of the virtues of the Qur'an and threatened those who turn away from following it, while also addressing the rejection of their objection that it contains abrogation of some of their laws. So He said: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment﴾. That is, in the same wondrous manner We sent down the Qur'an, comprising the foundations of the laws and their branches. It was also said: the meaning is: just as We sent down the Books to the messengers in their own languages, so We sent down to you the Qur'an in the tongue of the Arabs. By "judgment" is meant the rulings it contains, or an Arabic wisdom translated into the language of the Arabs. The accusative of "judgment" is in the sense of a circumstantial state (hal).

﴿And if you follow their desires﴾, which they seek from you as agreement with them in them, such as your continuing to face their qiblah and not opposing them in anything they believe, ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, which Allah has taught you, ﴿you will have no protector from Allah﴾, that is, no ally from His side to take charge of your affairs and support you, ﴿nor any shield﴾ to protect you from His punishment. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but it is an implicit warning to his community. The lam in "and if you follow" is the lam that introduces an oath.

"You will have no protector" (ma laka) stands in place of the answer to both the oath and the conditional.

﴿And We had already sent messengers before you and gave them wives and offspring﴾. That is, the messengers We sent before you were of the race of humankind; they had wives from among women, and they had offspring who multiplied from them and from their wives. We did not send as messengers angels who do not marry and have no offspring.

In this is a refutation of those who objected to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) marrying women; that is, this is the condition of the messengers of God who were sent before this Messenger, so why do you object to him for what they themselves did? ﴿It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah﴾, that is, it was not for any messenger among the messengers to bring any of the signs, among which is what the disbelievers proposed to him, except by the permission of Allah, glorified is He.

In this is a refutation of the disbelievers, who proposed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) signs of the kind they proposed, as already mentioned. ﴿For every term there is a Book﴾, that is, for every matter which Allah has decreed, or for every time in which Allah has decreed that a matter occurs, there is a Book with Allah that He records for His servants and by which He judges them.

al-Farra' said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, and the meaning is: "For every Book there is a term," that is, for every matter which Allah has written there is a fixed term and a known time, like His words, glorified is He: ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾ [al-An'am: 67]. The matter is not according to the will of the disbelievers and their proposals, but according to what He wills and chooses.

﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes﴾, that is, He effaces from that Book and establishes what He wills from it. It is said: "I erased the book (mahawtu al-kitab) with erasure" when you remove its trace.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read "yuthabbita" with light (tashdid absent). The rest read it with emphasis (tashdid). Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading.

The apparent sense of the Qur'anic wording is generality in everything that is in the Book, so He effaces what He wills to efface of misery or happiness, provision or lifespan, good or evil, and replaces this with that, and places this in the stead of that: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23]. To this view went 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Wa'il, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj and others. It was said: the verse is specific to happiness and misery. It was said: He effaces from the register of the recording angels what has no reward or punishment and establishes what contains reward and punishment. It was said: He effaces what He wills of provision. It was said: He effaces from the term of life. It was said: He effaces what He wills of the laws, abrogating it, and establishes what He wills so He does not abrogate it. It was said: He effaces what He wills of the sins of His servants and leaves what He wills. It was said: He effaces what He wills of sins through repentance and leaves what He wills of them without repentance. It was said: He effaces fathers and establishes sons. It was said: He effaces the moon and establishes the sun, like His words: ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day visible﴾ [al-Isra': 12]. It was said: He effaces, of the souls which He takes during sleep, what He wills, so that He causes its owner to die, and establishes what He wills, so He returns it to its owner. It was said: He effaces what He wills of generations and establishes what He wills of them. It was said: He effaces the world and establishes the Hereafter. Other views were also said which need not be mentioned. The first view is the best, as is indicated by the word "what" (ma) in His words "what He wills," which carries generality, together with the earlier mention of the Book in His words ﴿For every term there is a Book﴾, and together with His words ﴿and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾, that is, its origin, which is the Preserved Tablet. The meaning of the verse is that He effaces what He wills of what is in the Preserved Tablet, so it becomes as if nonexistent, and establishes what He wills of what is in it, so His decree and destiny take effect in it according to what His will requires. This does not contradict what is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in his saying: "The pen has dried." It was also said: those who rejoice are the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitabayn), because it agrees with what is in their books and confirms it. According to the first view, the intended meaning of His words, ﴿And among the factions are those who deny part of it﴾, is those among the Jews and Christians who did not embrace Islam. According to the second view, the intended meaning is the polytheists of Mecca and those like them; or it refers to some of the People of the Two Books, that is, of their factions, for they denied it because it contains abrogation of their laws. So the joy of those among them who rejoiced turns toward what agrees with what is in the two Books, and the denial of those among them who denied turns toward what opposes them both.

It was also said: the Book is the Qur'an, those who rejoice in it are the Muslims, and the factions are those who banded together against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from among the polytheists, Jews and Christians. The "part" they deny is whatever opposes what they themselves believe, according to the differences in their beliefs.

This was objected to: the joy of the Muslims at the revelation of the Qur'an is well known, so there is no benefit in mentioning it. It was answered that what is meant is an increase in joy and rejoicing.

Many commentators said: 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and those among the People of the Book who believed with him were distressed by the scarcity of the mention of al-Rahman in the Qur'an, given how often He is mentioned in the Torah. So God sent down ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon al-Rahman﴾ [al-Isra: 110], and they rejoiced at that. So He said: ﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him﴾, meaning, I do not associate with Him in any way. That is, say to them, O Muhammad, as a establishing of the proof and a rejection of their denial: I have only been commanded, in what has been revealed to me, to worship Allah and to affirm His oneness. This is a matter on which all the revealed laws agree, and on which all the religions that follow the messengers concur in not denying it.

The readers agreed on the accusative of "and not associate with Him" as a conjunction with "worship" (a'budu). Abu Khulayd read it in the nominative as a new sentence, and this reading was transmitted from Nafi'. The meaning would then be: "I call (adu'u) to Allah," that is, to Allah alone and not to other than Him, or to what I have been commanded, which is worshipping Allah alone. The first reading is better, because of His words ﴿and to Him is my return﴾, since the pronoun refers to Allah, glorified is He, meaning: to Him alone, not to other than Him, is my return.

Then He mentioned some of the virtues of the Qur'an and threatened those who turn away from following it, while also addressing the rejection of their objection that it contains abrogation of some of their laws. So He said: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment﴾. That is, in the same wondrous manner We sent down the Qur'an, comprising the foundations of the laws and their branches. It was also said: the meaning is: just as We sent down the Books to the messengers in their own languages, so We sent down to you the Qur'an in the tongue of the Arabs. By "judgment" is meant the rulings it contains, or an Arabic wisdom translated into the language of the Arabs. The accusative of "judgment" is in the sense of a circumstantial state (hal).

﴿And if you follow their desires﴾, which they seek from you as agreement with them in them, such as your continuing to face their qiblah and not opposing them in anything they believe, ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, which Allah has taught you, ﴿you will have no protector from Allah﴾, that is, no ally from His side to take charge of your affairs and support you, ﴿nor any shield﴾ to protect you from His punishment. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but it is an implicit warning to his community. The lam in "and if you follow" is the lam that introduces an oath.

"You will have no protector" (ma laka) stands in place of the answer to both the oath and the conditional.

﴿And We had already sent messengers before you and gave them wives and offspring﴾. That is, the messengers We sent before you were of the race of humankind; they had wives from among women, and they had offspring who multiplied from them and from their wives. We did not send as messengers angels who do not marry and have no offspring.

In this is a refutation of the disbelievers, who proposed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) signs of the kind they proposed, as already mentioned. ﴿For every term there is a Book﴾, that is, for every matter which Allah has decreed, or for every time in which Allah has decreed that a matter occurs, there is a Book with Allah that He records for His servants and by which He judges them.

It was said: He effaces what He wills of the laws, abrogating it, and establishes what He wills so He does not abrogate it. It was said: He effaces what He wills of sins through repentance and leaves what He wills of them without repentance. It was said: He effaces fathers and establishes sons. It was also said: those who rejoice are the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitabayn), because it agrees with what is in their books and confirms it. According to the first view, the intended meaning of His words, ﴿And among the factions are those who deny part of it﴾, is those among the Jews and Christians who did not embrace Islam. According to the second view, the intended meaning is the polytheists of Mecca and those like them; or it refers to some of the People of the Two Books, that is, of their factions, for they denied it because it contains abrogation of their laws. So the joy of those among them who rejoiced turns toward what agrees with what is in the two Books, and the denial of those among them who denied turns toward what opposes them both.

It was also said: the Book is the Qur'an, those who rejoice in it are the Muslims, and the factions are those who banded together against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from among the polytheists, Jews and Christians. The "part" they deny is whatever opposes what they themselves believe, according to the differences in their beliefs.

This was objected to: the joy of the Muslims at the revelation of the Qur'an is well known, so there is no benefit in mentioning it. It was answered that what is meant is an increase in joy and rejoicing.

Many commentators said: 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and those among the People of the Book who believed with him were distressed by the scarcity of the mention of al-Rahman in the Qur'an, given how often He is mentioned in the Torah. This is a matter on which all the revealed laws agree, and on which all the religions that follow the messengers concur in not denying it.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 13, verses 40–43:**

The *ma* in وإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ is extra (*zā'idah*), and the original form is: وإنْ نُرِكَ ﴿some of what We promise them﴾ of the punishment, as We promised them that by Our saying: ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 34], and by Our saying ﴿A calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieve, because of what they have done﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 31]. The meaning is: We show you some of what We promise them before your death, or We take you (in death) before showing you that. ﴿Your duty is only to convey (the message)﴾, that is, you are only required to convey the rulings of the message, and it is not incumbent upon you that they respond to what you have conveyed to them. ﴿And upon Us is the reckoning﴾, that is, calling them to account for their deeds and recompensing them for them, and this is not your responsibility. This is a consolation from Allah, glorified is He, to His Messenger (ﷺ), and an informing him that he has done what Allah commanded him to do, and that nothing else is required of him, and that whoever does not respond to his call and does not affirm his prophethood, Allah, glorified is He, will call him to account for what he has committed and dared upon.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 13, verses 40–43:**

The *ma* in وإمّا نُرِيَنَّكَ is extra (*zā'idah*), and the original form is: وإنْ نُرِكَ ﴿some of what We promise them﴾ of the punishment, as We promised them that by Our saying: ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 34], and by Our saying ﴿A calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieve, because of what they have done﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 31]. The meaning is: We show you some of what We promise them before your death, or We take you (in death) before showing you that. ﴿Your duty is only to convey (the message)﴾, that is, you are only required to convey the rulings of the message, and it is not incumbent upon you that they respond to what you have conveyed to them. ﴿And upon Us is the reckoning﴾, that is, calling them to account for their deeds and recompensing them for them, and this is not your responsibility. This is a consolation from Allah, glorified is He, to His Messenger (ﷺ), and an informing him that he has done what Allah commanded him to do, and that nothing else is required of him, and that whoever does not respond to his call and does not affirm his prophethood, Allah, glorified is He, will call him to account for what he has committed and dared upon.

﴿Do they not see﴾: that is, the people of Makkah, and the interrogative is for denunciation, meaning: Have they not looked ﴿that We come to the land, reducing it from its borders﴾? That is, We come to the land of disbelief, such as Makkah, reducing it from its borders by the conquests of the Muslims over it, little by little.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah informed that the clarification of what He promised the polytheists of their subjugation has become manifest. He says: Have they not seen that We have granted the Muslims conquest over the land, which has become clear to them? So how do they not take heed? It was also said: the meaning of the verse is the death of the scholars and the righteous.

Al-Qushayri said: According to this, *al-atrāf* (the borders) means the nobles, and Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-ṭaraf* is the noble man.

Al-Qurtubi said: This view is far-fetched, because the intent of the verse is: We showed them the decline in their affairs so that they would know that the delay of punishment from them is not due to incapacity. Unless it is understood as the death of the rabbis of the Jews and the Christians. It was also said: the intent of the verse is the ruin of the inhabited land until civilization is only in one area of it. It was said: the intent is the destruction of those nations who were destroyed. It was said: the intent is the decrease of the land's fruits. It was said: the intent is the oppression of its rulers until it diminishes.

﴿And Allah judges; there is none to repel His judgment﴾: that is, He judges as He wills concerning His creation, so He elevates this one and lowers that one, gives life to this one and causes that one to die, enriches this one and impoverishes that one. He has judged for the might of Islam and its supremacy over the religions. The clause ﴿there is none to repel His judgment﴾ is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). It was said: it is a parenthetical clause. The *mu'aqqib* is the one who turns back upon a thing and nullifies it; its real meaning is one who follows it up with rejection and nullification.

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is: there is no one who repels His judgment. He said: The *mu'aqqib* is one who follows a thing and overtakes it, and no one overtakes Him in it. The intent of the verse is that no one can follow up Allah's judgment, glorified is He, with diminution or alteration. ﴿And He is swift in reckoning﴾, so He recompenses the doer of good for his good, and the doer of evil for his evil, swiftly.

﴿Those before them had already schemed, but to Allah belongs all scheming﴾: that is, the disbelievers before the disbelievers of Makkah had already schemed against those whom Allah sent to them of the messengers, so they plotted against them and disbelieved in them. This is a consolation from Allah, glorified is He, to His Messenger (ﷺ), in which He informs him that this is the custom of the disbelievers from ancient times with the messengers of Allah, glorified is He. Then He informed him that their scheming is like nothing, and that all scheming belongs to Allah. So He said: ﴿So to Allah belongs all scheming﴾: the scheming of others is not counted. Then Allah, glorified is He, explained this scheming which is established for Him alone, saying: ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾, of good and evil, and recompenses it accordingly. Whoever knows what every soul earns and prepares its recompense for it, all scheming is his, because it comes upon them from where they do not perceive.

Al-Wahidi said: The scheming of schemers is created, so it does not harm except by His will. It was also said: the meaning is: to Allah belongs the recompense of the scheming of schemers. ﴿And the disbeliever will know for whom is the ultimate abode.﴾ Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited *al-kāfiru* (the disbeliever) in the singular, while the rest recited *al-kuffār* (the disbelievers) in the plural. That is: the category of the disbeliever will know for whom the praiseworthy outcome is, from the two groups, in the abode of this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both. It was said: the intent of *al-kāfir* is Abu Jahl.

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "You are not a messenger."﴾ That is, the polytheists, or all the disbelievers, say: O Muhammad, you are not a messenger from Allah to the people. So Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them, and He said: ﴿Say: "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you"﴾, for He knows the truth of my messengership and the veracity of my call, and He knows your lying. ﴿And whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾: that is, knowledge of the category of the Book, such as the Torah and the Gospel, for its people who are knowledgeable in them know the truth of the messengership of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Those among them who embraced Islam have informed of this, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Salman al-Farisi, Tamim al-Dari and others like them. The polytheists of the Arabs used to ask the People of the Book and refer to them, so Allah, glorified is He, guided them in this verse to the fact that the People of the Book know this. It was also said: the intent of the Book is the Qur'an, and whoever has knowledge of it are the Muslims.
